speechtext:

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions pf Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Whereas the concerns of new immigrants were illustrated by the Canadian Federation of Vietnamese Associations at their recent meeting in Ottawa when they unanimously passed several resolutions regarding resettlement assistance and language training, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Heap)-and I am sure this motion will have the unanimous support of the House:
That the federal government, in the preparation of its immigration levels paper and settlement policy take into account and consider, first, providing financial support to the Vietnamese Association projects of training resettlement workers with a background in legal matters; second, supporting a training program of Vietnamese community workers; third, improving and extending the period of language training; fourth, providing a minimum of 24 weeks of language training with living allowances, regardless of their sponsorship, and fifth, inviting ethnic communities to participate in the formulation of language training policies for immigrants and refugees.

Considering the thousands of automotive workers who have been laid off for an indefinite period at Boisbriand, Oshawa, Windsor and Oakville, and considering the failure of the Liberal government to conclude an agreement with Japan on what would constitute an equitable share of the Canadian automobile market, and the government's inability to bring down interest rates, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, given the unprecedented outflow of investment capital from Canada which grew by 500 per cent in 1981 to almost $20 billion, while our foreign borrowing has increased by more than $30 billion secured by way of bonds and loans with foreign lenders who enjoy guaranteed rates of return of 16 per cent to 20 per cent annually, and whereas the antiinvestment policies of the federal Liberals are the principal cause of widespread unemployment, high domestic interest rates, and untold human misery everywhere in Canada, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley (Mr. McCuish):
That the government be directed to restore economic confidence by reversing immediately its anti-investment policies embodied in FIRA, the NEP, and the illegitimate November 12 budget or, barring such a reversal, the government is hereby instructed to resign.

Madam Speaker, as usual the Deputy Prime Minister talks a good battle. He has come back from a conference which did in fact lead to the Prime Minister recognizing in Versailles that there was an economic crisis in Canada for which we can at least be thankful.
I have a specific question and a proposal, assuming that the Deputy Prime Minister takes seriously the words that he reiterated just now, that the government is committed to growth and employment in terms of new policies. Considering that there are roughly three days of debating time left on energy bills which we have all discussed and debated before, and also considering that there are three days allocated to opposition parties remaining in this session, I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister is the government now prepared to come to grips in a serious and immediate way with the economic problems of this country, by introducing, say, next Monday, specific economic measures to which we could allocate a full week's time of debate, if the opposition parties gave up their days for debate on other matters so that we could get on with dealing with the economic crisis.

here in 1967 when the act in question was adopted. The issue was thoroughly debated at that time. speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, June 7, 1982, consideration of Bill C-103, to amend the Petroleum Administration Act and to enact provisions related thereto, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation, and Motion No. 6 (Mr. Hawkes).

Madam Speaker, I want to speak in support of the amendment proposed. Debate on the amendment was opened by my colleague, the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre). When one looks at the amendment, one will recognize that it is a fairly simple and straightforward amendment but, most of all, it is a very reasonable amendment. It is responsible and contains a great deal of common sense. The amendment proposes to limit the
801 16-18

June 8, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
amount of money that can be collected under the Canadian ownership account. According to Clause 39, which deals with Section 65.26(3)(b) of the act as set out on page 29 of the bill, the money provided by the collection of this surcharge can be used as follows:
-for investment in shares, debentures, bonds or other evidences of indebtedness of or for property acquisitions from any person in order to increase Canadian public ownership of the oil and gas industry in Canada and to repay loans or expenses incurred for that purpose.
The amendment would place a limit on the revenue collected under the Canadian ownership charge of $1,460 billion. It is a sunset provision, in effect. Parliamentary approval would be required before any wild and woolly deals such as the Petrofina deal could be made. In this clause the government seeks carte blanche approval to buy a company outright, to buy shares in a company or to buy properties without parliamentary approval. It could use its authority to draw upon a slush fund to be created at the expense of the consumers of Canada in order to buy a greater percentage of the oil industry. Considering the present lack of control we have over Crown corporations and the accountability of the government, I think this amendment deserves to be considered.
What the government is really saying is that state takeover is a way of Canadian life; that it has become part and parcel of the social and economic fabric of our society; that the government has the power and in its wisdom it shall decide when, where and how it shall penetrate the oil industry and how much it shall pay for it without being accountable to the people of Canada or making any reference to Parliament.
My colleague's amendment deserves consideration by all members of the House, Mr. Speaker. If the institution of Parliament is to be preserved and its credibility enhanced, then it must uphold its responsibility for funds held in trust for the Canadian people. Parliament must have the final say in this connection.
There are other areas that I want to touch on briefly, such as the economic climate in the country which is closely tied to the fundamental principles of the National Energy Program and the budget. There is no question that the country is in very serious economic trouble and there are many reasons for this. I would be the first to admit that the international environment is part of the problem but I do not think it is the only reason. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and his colleagues on the treasury benches will have to accept their responsibility for the present ills of the country. They cannot continue to plead that it is an international problem and an offshoot of the policies of the United States. I say very bluntly that the problems we face in this country are largely made-in-Canada problems and require made-in-Canada solutions.
There are three components that I believe contribute to the current malaise. The first is a psychological or attitudinal problem. There is a negative psychology in the country which pervades all aspects of our society and all regions of the country. The record of the government in the last two years has created this negativism. It has created a feeling of deep
mistrust and now Canadians do not believe anything that the government says any more.
A week ago the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) announced changes to the National Energy Program. However, people in the industry are so cynical now that they do not believe that the minister's intentions or the intentions of the government are honourable. These provisions are to be in effect for a limited time only. But the fundamental philosophy enshrined in the National Energy Program was not withdrawn; it was a patchwork scheme drawn up to attract a certain amount of support. There may be support in some sectors of the industry but, by and large, the damage has been done. The goose that laid the golden egg that was our once vibrant industry has been killed. It will take more than the announcement made by the minister to revive it.
There is a mood of cynicism in the country. When people remember that the government fought an election on a platform of cheap energy and that in less than two years it has doubled the price of gasoline, it is not surprising that no one believes it any more. Today the Minister of Finance reiterated that the government has a mandate from the people of Canada, but that mandate was obtained on a platform of lies and deceit. If the people of Canada had a second chance, knowing as they do now that the government did not mean what it said, I am sure the results would be quite different. There is a feeling of deep mistrust in the country and a realization that the government would rather confront than co-operate. This has led to division and mistrust rather than to harmony.
Another aspect of this attitudinal problem is that more and more Canadians now realize that the government is incompetent. It does not have answers. It has destroyed the incentive, the desire, to progress that was once alive in the country. It has destroyed industries that were once humming and viable. There is a growing realization that the government is incompetent and is largely responsible for the mess we are in, that it does not understand what makes the country tick or what makes the economy tick. It has run out of solutions.
Rather than having a positive mood in the country and a readiness to tackle urgent economic problems, there is a feeling of hopelessness, despair and helplessness around us. There is uncertainty, confusion, and investment decisions are being postponed. Things are going in reverse, Mr. Speaker.
There is a general view abroad in the country that, given our resources and the opportunities that exist for individuals, companies, entrepreneurs and investors, we should all be doing much better. But the government has stymied initiative; it has stymied investment; it has stymied the entrepreneurial spirit that was the hallmark of this country over the last 20 or 30 years.
Another reason for our present problems is the economic policy of the government which is reflected in the philosophy of the budget. That budget, as we all know-and we are not sure whether it will survive this Parliament-stifles growth,
June 8, 1982

discourages investment, penalizes initiative and enterprise, and advocates greater state control in the growth and development of economic opportunity in Canada. It was interesting to note that Mr. W. P. Wilder, the president and chief executive officer of Hiram Walker Resources Ltd., in a speech to the Canadian Club of Montreal on March 1, said this:
The biggest single barrier to investment-whether it be the multi-million dollar investments called for by the energy industry or the smaller investments required in other industries across the country-is uncertainty. And this federal government, through its over-all approach to the economy, has raised a basic uncertainty as to whether or not investment in Canada-by Canadians or by anybody else-is really a very good idea in business terms.
I think that summarizes very succinctly the prevailing mood in the minds of investors.
The third issue which has led to the deterioration in our economy is, naturally, the NEP. The fact that we are engaged in this rather long debate, Mr. Speaker, which strikes at the very core of the NEP, is certainly a tribute to my colleague, the hon. member for Calgary Centre, and indeed to the House leader of my party. I think it is fair to say that the NEP is not fully understood by the average Canadian, and hopefully through this debate we will be able to apprise Canadians in a more general way as to the real thrust of the NEP, what it has done and failed to do, and how it might be improved.
The short and simple solution would be to have the whole thing withdrawn and to start all over again. I think that would do a lot to lift confidence and improve the investment climate, particularly in the oil sector. Those are not only my views, they are shared by other learned individuals in the country. I would like to quote from an article written by Mr. John Meyer, a very well-known journalist, who has written some very learned articles on the economy, energy, and business in general. This is from an article which appeared in The Executive magazine of April, 1982 and is entitled-and this is the very point I am trying to make-"Canada's collapse began with the NEP". He goes on to say:
This is a recession which need never have happened. Now that it has, it looks as if it will last longer and hurt more than any previous post-war recession. After three quarters, there is still no end to it in sight.
This recession was triggered and has since been intensified by a succession of federal measures and, to a lesser extent, the provincial responses they evoked. The breaking point came with the National Energy Program.
To attribute this recession to the arrival together of most of the developed countries on the same downslope of the business cycle, or to attribute it to high U.S. interest rates, is to ignore the dominant role of energy among our other natural resources.
Provision for a competitive rate of return on oil and gas production would have strengthened the dollar, improved national productivity and raised the national income. At most, it could have overtaken the deterrents of high interest rates and slumping other countries. At least it would have offered the promise of early recovery. The introduction of the NEP deprived us of both.
Before NEP, the strongly rising volume of investment in oil and gas exploration and development had been driving the whole economy forward. Every dollar invested by the petroleum industry multiplied two or three times through the economy in purchases of equipment and services.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, the purchase of equipment and services not only in western Canada, but indeed throughout all of Canada. I quote again:
Since NEP, the industry's investment here has been drastically reduced, by 30 per cent to 40 per cent through 1981 and by at least that much again this year.
Petroleum Administration Act
These are not now recoverable funds. They have either been committed outside Canada or absorbed by government.
He goes on to say:
For the better part of a decade, government has been reaching out to capture key elements in the economy, to transform them into instruments for implementing its vision of the corporate state-that is, one in which political authority is assured by control over investment and production.
An earlier model of the corporate state was Mussolini's Italy of the late 1920s and 1930s. But set aside what the attempts to emulate it here imply for individual rights and freedoms. Consider only what it has cost so far in forfeited economic growth.
I can quote Mr. Wilder again where he says in his speech to the Canadian Club of Montreal:
And the main point I want to make-a point I do not believe the energy industry has made as clearly as it should have-is that the NEP is not an isolated set of government policies that affect the oil and gas industry alone. The NEP is just one part of an approach to the economy of this country on the part of the federal government that is undermining the ability of every industry in Canada to meet the kinds of economic challenges it faces today.
He goes on to say that:
In total, because of the NEP, the energy industry is smaller, and weaker, and less capable of finding the new energy sources we will need to achieve selfsufficiency in Canada.
He goes on to talk about trust:
The people in our industry are less and less disposed to trust the federal government.
He then talks about Canadianization:
-"Canadianized" industry is going to be much smaller than it would have been under more advantageous conditions.
So the things we are espousing here today have not simply been dreamed up by members on this side of the House. The fact of the matter is that they are shared by many other knowledgeable people throughout the country. Simply put, we can summarize the NEP as being the most destructive measure ever perpetrated on a once viable industry in Canada. It has literally destroyed the western oil industry. Exploration is down by 40 per cent, over 200 rigs have left the country, we have massive lay-offs, bankruptcies, and employment is down by 33 per cent. More than 14,000 people have lost their jobs in the energy industry since the NEP came into being. There has been an exodus of capital, something like $18 billion in 1981. Over $1 billion worth of machines have left this country in the form of drilling rigs and equipment. We have auction sales every day. As my colleague the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) has indicated, those sales produce 50 cents on the dollar and certainly that is eroding confidence in the industry and in the economy as a whole. On May 21, 1980, two years ago, there were over 400 drilling rigs working in western Canada. Today there are fewer than 100. Those rigs are like little factories for us in western Canada; they employ 40 to 50 people each. Where have they gone? They have gone south of the border, and some young men and women have been fortunate enough to go with them. They found jobs there and the United States gave them work permits.
I can go on. The cancellation of megaprojects is clearly another example of the disaster which has been caused by the NEP. We are more reliant on imported oil today than we were a year ago. And what are we doing? We are importing oil

June 8, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
while shutting in our own domestic sources of supply. Something in the order of 200,000 to 300,000 barrels a day are shut in. Those wells are not pumping so they do not require service, and that is adding to the unemployment rolls, further eroding our balance of payments, weakening our dollar, increasing interest rates, and contributing to the declining confidence in the Canadian economy.
There can be no question that the disastrous NEP has not yet completed its work in the country. The fact of the matter is that its effects are now spreading to the petrochemical industry. In the province of Alberta at the end of 1981 there was a value of $8 billion placed on some 15 petrochemical projects which were identified as having the potential for development. What has happened? A number of things have happened. What with excessive taxation and the National Energy Program, the competitive edge for Alberta's ethane price no longer exists. Feedstock prices in the United States are considerably less and as a result some 15 projects worth $8 billion have been thrown into jeopardy. They are either on hold, postponed indefinitely or have been dropped. That is the kind of climate that exists.
I spoke earlier of confidence. Some people ask how we can restore confidence in the country. There are some people who believe that confidence will not be restored until the Liberals leave the treasury benches of government. Mr. Roy Farran on April 16 wrote the following in the Edmonton Journal under the heading: "When the Liberals go, oil industry will recover". Mr. Farran's article reads:
Politicians would do an enormous favour to the nation if they would quit lying and start telling the truth. Any chance of Canada's becoming energy selfsufficient before 1990 has been blown long ago.
What do you think it means when Imperial pulls out of a petrochemical plant near Edmonton, when half the companies withdraw from the third oil sands plant, when Imperial disperses its team at Cold Lake, when Shell sells off subsidiaries, when oil lease sales drop by half?
Why do you think Alberta Energy shares fell from $25 to $10?
I suppose there are still pipedreamers up there at the university who will say with a straight face that the oil companies are only bluffing for more. And they'll base their argument on some figure thrown out by Lalonde or Leitch during the energy battle even though by now it is quite clear that neither of them knew what they were talking about.
His article continues:
They really did kill the goose that laid the golden eggs, didn't they?
Mr. Farran goes on to say:
Canada is now feeling the joy commonly experienced in the Third World when hated multinationals are driven out. The euphoria of liberation is marvellous. Then come withdrawal pains as they learn too late that these gringos or foreign dogs did bring benefits, too-
The most that can be said is it could have been a lot worse if Alberta had not fought so hard. But the pact was no great day for Canada, believe me.
Only when the Liberals go will it be time to peal the bells. For everything they touch goes bad.
That feeling is very predominant, particularly in western Canada and to an increasing degree in other parts of Canada. What this government has done to the oil industry it is doing to other industries as well. Look what it has done to the dollar.
What this government has done to the oil industry and to the dollar will also happen to Canadians. This government will inflict serious damage and hardship on them.
When we look at the value of our dollar these days we can only identify that, through the process of Canadianization, the National Energy Program and the budget, we have had a tremendous outflow of Canadian dollars which has caused the reduction in the value of our dollar, making it necessary to raise interest rates to attract sufficient capital into the country. The investment dollars which left the country are no longer here to stimulate industry and the economy, to retool, to improve our productivity, to engage in greater research and development which enabled Canada to be more productive and competitive in the international marketplace. Everything this government has touched has gone sour.
The National Energy Program is a clear example of that. Back in 1980 Canada's energy industry was coming along. It was going great. There was an agreement initialled and ready to be signed. The Alsands project was going ahead. The Cold Lake project was going ahead. The heavy oil upgrader project was going ahead. There was a mood of optimism. There was a feeling that we would finally achieve the goal of energy selfsufficiency. There would have been benefits for all Canadians, not only for western Canadians. Before the ink was dry on the Syncrude contract, some $250 million worth of contracts were let to the province of Ontario for the machinery and equipment that were necessary to see that project go ahead. The $14 billion or $15 billion oil sands plant would have created some $7 billion worth of economic activity for Ontario. Everyone would have benefited. We would have been more secure. We would have had a greater level of employment. There would have been a positive attitude in the country rather than the negative attitude we have today.
I want to talk briefly about Canadianization, which is really the thrust of this motion. The clause we are now dealing with is the heart and core of the whole question of Canadianization. No one will argue with the objective of increasing Canadian ownership in any industry, particularly the oil industry. I support it and my party supports it. It is a laudable objective, there is no question about that. But in the process of this government implementing its program of Canadianization, it has literally destroyed the very basic component of Canadian enterprise within the energy sector, that is, the exploration and service sector. That industry has been crippled and destroyed as a result of the policies of the National Energy Program. It was an industry that was almost totally Canadian owned. We have expertise in drilling and exploration, in manufacturing and indeed in the servicing area.
In terms of dealing with the heavy oil tar sands and the various methods and the technology that we have, I believe we are second to none in the world. But with the killing of the Cold Lake project, with the killing of the Alsands project and the delay in moving ahead with the heavy oil upgrader, our technical expertise is getting less and less.
June 8, 1982

The same thing applies to the service and exploration sector. As a result of the National Energy Program and the government's commitment to Canadianization, what has happened? Every day a new outfit goes into receivership or bankruptcy. I will give one example of this. A company called Raydan Transport Ltd., an oilfield trucking company based in Nisku just south of Edmonton, owned a fleet of 39 trucks. It employed 105 people full-time and it hired 36 casual workers when necessary. By last December the company had auctioned all but one truck and the staff had been reduced to four. That is one of the results of Canadianization and the National Energy Program.
During the last week in May in the city of Lloydminster, which is in my constituency, 200 oil industry jobs were thrown into jeopardy. In the Toronto Star we read:
The jobs of 200 Lloydminster residents were thrown into jeopardy after Universal Industries Ltd. announced it has been placed in receivership yesterday. The company, which manufactures oil-pumping units, faces financial difficulties due to the continuing economic uncertainty surrounding the Canadian oil and gas industry.

When the creation of Petro-Canada was being debated, there was a recognition of the fact that there would probably have to be public funds injected into those areas of Canada, such as the frontier, heavy oil areas and offshore areas, since the private sector may not be eager to go into those areas. Therefore, one of the primary objectives in creating Petro-Canada was to use it as an instrument to further enhance the security of supply in Canada and to further assist in achieving the goal of oil and gas self-sufficiency.
The second objective was essentially to ensure and promote a more rapid pace of oil sands research and development as a potential back-up source of energy supply for Canada.

Control and accountability of Crown corporations has been a major concern of this office for a number of years. Mr. Speaker, 1 had not intended to participate in our discussion this afternoon, but after listening to some of the remarks of the hon. member opposite who has just spoken, I want to make one or two comments. I listened to the hon. member with the respect which I normally accord to him, because he has made a number of very useful contributions to our debates in the past. But I thought that this afternoon he failed in some respects to maintain that standard by introducing material which was either erroneous or anachronistic in some ways irrelevant to the legislation we have before us. In particular, I have in mind the discussion in which the hon. member engaged with regard to that part of the legislation referring to the petroleum compensation charge and the related question of a shut-in oil industry.
I am sure the hon. member opposite would recognize that over the years the amount of shut-in oil in Canada has varied depending on marketing and other circumstances. But as we all recognize, the amount of shut-in oil in Canada substantially increased during a recent period. Indeed, the government quite clearly stated in the National Energy Program update of a fortnight ago that it considers it essential that Canadian domestic oil be used to meet Canadian needs and that it has been deeply concerned about the level of shut-in oil which has existed in recent months. So there is no disagreement in the House or, indeed, across Canada in general that the amount of shut-in oil has been high and that measures should be taken to reduce it.
When the government did recognize that a problem was emerging earlier this year, it announced on April 1 certain actions which have considerably alleviated the problem. However, for a moment I want to touch on some of the reasons the problem occurred and then on some of the solutions which have been put in place.
Initially, some part of the shut-in oil resulted from the cutbacks in production which the Government of Alberta instituted as part of its response to the National Energy Program. Oil companies understandably moved at that time to offset the cutback in Alberta production by seeking the guarantee, the assurance, of offshore supply. Those contracts, of course, simply could not be cancelled or reneged upon in a very brief period. Some of them have already run their course and others will in the near future.
Second, a contributing factor has been a lower demand in the United States for Canadian heavy oils. The recession in the United States has resulted in lower demand for heavy oils surplus to Canadian needs which have been exported to the United States. The result has been additional shut-in oil in western Canada.
Third, of course, has been the reduction in demand here in Canada for refined petroleum products.
Some mention was made earlier, in our discussions of the National Energy Program, of its success in reducing the demand for oil. One of the ramifications of that success has been that within Canada there has been a drop-off in demand for certain types of oil. The eastern refiners have necessarily had to vary their mix of imported oils to match demands in Canada and that, in turn, has had its impact on the shut-in oil problem.
Fourth, some refiners took advantage of lower international oil prices in recent months. A few Canadian refiners have taken advantage of those lower international prices to reduce their costs. That has meant, in some instances, passing up Canadian supply in favour of imported oil. All those factors come together and have contributed to a situation where we have had significant amounts of shut-in oil.
As I mentioned, the government moved on April 1 to ensure that there would be greater use made of our own domestic sources of oil and to ensure that imported oil was not used to displace Canadian oil. On April 1, measures were announced to ensure that heavy oil surpluses were competitively priced in the U.S. market. The National Energy Board took steps to issue licences for the export of such oil for 12 months rather than for shorter periods which had been in place in the past. Additionally, the government moved to encourage eastern Canadian refiners to import only minimum offshore amounts so as to help ensure that Canadian sources were used in place of imported oil.
As a result of those and other measures there has been a quite dramatic drop in the amount of shut-in oil in Canada. There was, in fact, a period in April when shut-in oil amounted to some 65,000 cubic metres. Two months later, in June, that amount has dropped to 5,400 cubic metres. That is, in two months it has dropped from 65,000 to 5,000. All hon. members will agree that that has been a dramatic and sudden reduction in shut-in oil, both of the conventional light and medium crudes, as well as heavy crudes. Now, that is not to say that the amount I have just cited for June, 5,400 cubic metres, will necessarily be the same amount for every month in the future, but it seems evident to me that we have seen a real turnaround in the situation which is very real. I would recommend that the hon. member who spoke before me look into the facts.
I agree that in July or later, during the early autumn, for example, when there is a traditional refinery shutdown for maintenance, there may be some temporary increase, possibly in the magnitude of 5,000 or 10,000 cubic metres of shut-in oil. However, I would submit that it would be nothing of the order of magnitude that we have seen in the past, due to the various measures taken.
I want to draw to the attention of the hon. member opposite the fact that not only on April 1 were measures taken by the

government to ensure that the use of Canadian oil was promoted, but also in the update of the National Energy Program there were a number of additional measures taken to ensure that a major growth in shut-in oil does not recur. I draw to the hon. member's attention the fact that the government has committed itself to restricting crude oil imports to those volumes under current contract necessary to preserve continued access to offshore oil.
Perhaps more important, adjustments will be made to the petroleum import compensation program, adjustments fully in accord with the legislation now before us, to ensure that the program is more responsive to offshore oil prices paid by Canadian importers.

producers. The count of active seismic crews, which performs the first step in exploration by mapping geologic strata with reflected soundwaves, has been declining for seven straight months in the U.S. Drilling rigs are "stacked" or out of service, all over the oil patch.

That is the sum total of those ten amendments, and let me deal with the one before us now. We have to read through all the legal language to find out that there is a tax of 4.5 cents a gallon. It does not sound like much, but when one fills up the gas tank in his car, it is a dollar. When we fill up our home heating oil tanks in the wintertime, the sum total of that 4.5 cents tax is $3 million a day. That 4.5 cents a gallon represents $3 million a day. Did the government have the courage to bring in a piece of legislation to say it would tax the people 4.5 cents a gallon until the government has collected enough money to pay for the buy-out of Petrofina and then it would stop that tax? No, it did not. No part of this legislation gives us any indication that when that purchase is completed the tax will stop.
The purpose of this amendment is to stop the tax once the buy-out is complete. If this amendment is adopted, the 4.5 cents a gallon tax would stop. But no, the Liberal Party wants to keep the tax in place forever. Four and a half cents a gallon is about 5 per cent of the cost of our home heating oil, about 5 per cent of the cost of the gasoline which goes into our cars and about 5 per cent of the cost of the gasoline which goes into tractors used in the production of food. This tax makes everything more expensive.
What is the government doing with this money? The first $1,460 million is to buy Petrofina. Canadians should think about that because what that means is that $1,460 million will be sent outside Canada, largely to the people who live in Belgium. People without jobs in Canada should stop and ask themselves whether their unemployment is partly because this government decided to send $1,460 million out of Canada for this one purpose alone. Do the people of Canada want the government to take 4.5 cents a gallon out of their pockets and send it out of the country? When the government does that, it
Petroleum Administration Act
drives down the value of our dollar. Today our dollar is worth just a little over 79 cents American. A few weeks ago it was worth about 83 cents American. When the value of the dollar falls four cents, practically everything we buy becomes more expensive. The cost of living goes up when this government sends dollars out of the country.
If we pay 4.5 cents tax on every gallon we buy, we might ask ourselves what we want the government to do with it. The 1.2 million Canadians who are unemployed today would like to see the government use that money to create jobs. Canadians who cannot afford their mortgages and are in danger of losing their homes would rather their government brought interest rates down a little so that they can keep their homes. Small-businessmen whose businesses are going bankrupt because of high interest rates would rather see the government take that 4.5 cents and reduce interest rates so they will not go bankrupt and all their employees will not lose their jobs. It is a matter of public choice. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, supported by all the backbenchers opposite, has decided to send that money out of the country, and he has decided to keep collecting 4.5 cents after the need for it is gone.
How can members of this House go home to their ridings this weekend and say they stood in the House of Commons and voted to impose a 4.5 cents a gallon tax on gasoline forever so that only the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources can decide how to spend it and so that he can send it out of the country? Instead of creating jobs in Canada, he has already decided to send money out of Canada to create jobs in Belgium. Where will he send money next? Will he create jobs in the United States of America? Will he create jobs in Mexico? Will he create jobs in Venezuela? The minister wants to take 4.5 cents per gallon out of my pocket to create jobs in other countries and not in this country where 1.2 million-plus Canadians are unemployed.
Members of Parliament have been sent to this place to help Canadians, and I urge them to vote for this amendment because, at the very least, it would stop this minister from collecting that $3 million a day and sending it out of Canada. If he does not have it, he cannot send it out. It would be wise in the current situation if we took that $3 million a day and spent it in Canada rather than in some other country. I wonder if there are 365 communities in Canada which could use $3 million each to help get projects started, to help get factories going, to reduce interest rates, to encourage businesses to develop and to create jobs. If the answer is yes, we have an opportunity today. All we have to do is vote for this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, very simply, this amendment seeks to make the bill read in the manner in which the government indicates it intends the legislation to impact on the Canadian economy. The amendment merely says that if in fact there is to be a Canadian ownership charge for the purpose of increasing Canadian ownership-which we do not think is justified, reasonable or appropriate-then the moneys collected should be spent to purchase assets, shares, capital and so forth of non-Canadian-owned oil and gas companies. We simply would change the wording of the appropriate clause to have the legislation do what the government tells us it is intended to do.
Frankly, I do not believe the government will go along with this amendment because I do not believe the government when it says its purpose is Canadianization. I do not think that is any more honest than a number of things the government has been telling us.
The purpose of this whole program is nationalization and state ownership. Big brother is going to run things for us, and that is going to make us very comfortable, secure and selfsufficient! The economy is going to be run by these genuises in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources who have made such a success of this country's energy industry so far that they have driven out $19 billion worth of capital, put thousands of people out of jobs and driven hundreds of companies to bankruptcy! That kind of performance will not deter the true ideologue and the trained donkeys who can be depended upon to support such behaviour. If state ownership is the object, I suppose that is what we will get because we cannot expect trained donkeys to learn from experience, but we continue to hope.
This amendment was put forward with a view to having the legislation reflect what the minister says it was intended to do. We will see whether he was telling us the truth or not when we see how the trained donkeys vote. I am quite confident that they will vote against it.
When speaking to motion No. 6 yesterday, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) made a couple of statements that I should like to correct. He suggested that we should read what Jeff Simpson had to say about Norway's Statoil and the Norwegian oil fields. I suggest that he do a little more reading himself. He would find out that in the last
June 8, 1982

few months the Norwegian government has changed the situation considerably and Statoil is no longer the big brother of the Norwegian oil fields. The Norwegians have learned, as we should have learned by now, that Crown corporations in Norway do not work any better than they work in Canada. The hammerlock that Statoil had on the Norwegian oil fields was offered to us as a model to be followed in giving Petro-Canada the same kind of hammerlock on Canada lands, but the Norwegians are changing the situation. They have learned that Crown corporations are not the answer. If were to follow Norway's example we would rescind some of the powers we have given to Petro-Canada, not increase them as the hon. member suggested.
The hon. member also made reference to Britain but I think he should inform himself on that situation as well. He would find that the British national oil company, which was created by the Labour government as a kind of big brother operation to run the British North Sea oil fields, has had its powers curtailed. In Britain, as in Canada, it was discovered that Crown corporations do not work. They do not work in Britain, they do not work in Norway, they do not work in Poland, they do not work in the Soviet Union-they just do not work. I would hope that even the obtuse members to my left would eventually learn that lesson.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway suggested that the Progressive Conservative Party was not being true to its roots when he read from a 1974 policy document in which the party indicated it was in favour of at least 50 per cent ownership of resource industries, including oil and gas. He should have kept reading that document as well. He would have found that among the specific suggestions made by the Progressive Conservative Party for changes in Canadian law that would promote Canadian ownership was a change in the income tax law which at that time contained something called the principal business test for oil and gas investment. Basically, that meant that unless you were already engaged in the oil and gas industry you would not receive the same incentives as those already engaged in it received. The impact was that an American, a German, a Swiss or a British company could drill a well in Canada with pre-tax dollars but Canadians could not. That was the absurd situation that existed in 1974 and for a decade before that. Canadians were at a disadvantage compared to foreigners when it came to investment in Canada. The Progressive Conservative Party was outraged and said that if that were changed there would be a tremendous increase in investment by Canadians in the oil and gas industry.
The provision was changed in the budget of December, 1975. From 1976 onward, for the first time, Canadians were on a par with foreigners regarding investment in the Canadian oil and gas industry. In 1975 the oil industry was 92 per cent foreign owned, but four years later it was only 72 per cent foreign owned. So Canadian ownership increased spectacularly as the result of that simple change in the tax law which was part of our policy in 1974 and was adopted by the government and put into effect in 1976.

The effect of the National Energy Program was to slow down Canadianization, not increase it. The federal Petroleum Monitoring Agency is proof of that. Any member of the House who is interested in what happened should read the latest report which shows that, as a result of the National Energy Program, in the first six months of 1981 foreign-owned companies operating in Canada suffered a loss of 28 per cent of their income while Canadian-owned oil and gas companies lost 52 per cent of their income. The National Energy Program is discouraging to foreign owners in the Canadian oil and gas industry but it is devastating to Canadians. It is an affront to honesty, integrity and decency for Liberals to claim that the National Energy Program is good for Canadianization. That is not the case, Mr. Speaker.
The New Democratic Party and the Liberals talk about Canadianization of the industry but they neglect to examine the whole spectrum of the industry. Their idea of Canadianization is how many service stations have red maple leaves painted on them.
A decade ago the drilling industry, which is an important part of the oil and gas industry, was as much as 80 per cent foreign owned. The big companies that dominated the industry were foreign owned. In 1980 the industry was 95 per cent Canadian owned. It had become Canadianized without big brother, without Crown corporations and without any of this nonsense about Liberal concern.
With a few super depletion allowances.
The hon. member speaks of super depletion. I am talking about the drilling industry. He does not even know what I am talking about.
Who do you think pays for all that? You and I, baby.

The energy critic for the NDP, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, talks about the super depletion allowance. That does not apply to provincial lands, it applies only to federal lands in the high Arctic. It applies only to wells in excess of $5 million each. The drilling industry does not really participate in those wells; they are drilled basically by the companies concerned. There has been in the order of 60 or 70 in total drilled in the high Arctic, and there has been only a dozen or so eligible for super depletion.
Now, in comparison, I am talking about the 5,000 wells drilled in provincial lands by Canadian drilling companies which were devastated by the NEP. They are now in Colorado, Texas or Kansas. As usual, the hon. member has his facts totally wrong and he shows why the monicker of "Liberal Party West" is appropriate. Facts are not going to get in the way of a good issue!
Another aspect of the industry is that of service companies. They go in after a well is drilled and service it. A decade ago that industry was overwhelmingly foreign owned; today it is overwhelmingly Canadian owned. That industry has been

Anyone who says, Mr. Speaker, that the NEP has contributed to Canadianization is a fool or a liar; one or the other. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a few remarks to make on this amendment. Before I do that, I want to put something on the record for the edification of members who were not privy to the deliberations which took place in the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation.
As we all know, there was a House order determining the length of this particular debate; the legislation had to be sent to committee and then returned to the chamber within a specified time frame. Throughout the process hon. members of the official opposition, the New Democratic Party and the government had an opportunity to review in depth the substance of the various pieces of legislation which were before the committee. In doing so, we called upon a good number of experts. We heard representations from the business and academic communities. A number of individuals put forward their ideas on the pith and substance of the legislation. There were a number of suggestions on how the legislation could be improved. There was some serious debate as to what different clauses meant or indeed what their effect would be.
I, like the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), am somewhat concerned, and perhaps in some respects annoyed, by the tone of the official opposition. However, perhaps that tone will continue because it has been part and parcel of its ideology and has been intensified as a result of the last federal election in February, 1980. Unfortunately the official opposition has not recovered from that particular defeat. It is attempting to use any means-and I use that phrase quite liberally-at its disposal in an attempt to recreate the situation which took place in 1979.
Hon. members of the official opposition have made a great many comments against Petro-Canada. It should be noted that according to my latest calculations they have approximately three positions on that Crown corporation. That may have changed; there may be four by the time we conclude this debate, but basically they have three positions. I believe Petro-Canada is something which the people of Canada want. It is important in terms of developing and promoting a national energy policy.
Hon. members opposite made reference to the fact that Petro-Canada is not a good company and is not needed. They have given it a whole host of descriptions. I should like to indicate for their edification that as a member of government I believe wholeheartedly that the people employed by Petro-Canada are extremely competent, concerned and dedicated public servants who believe very strongly in the National Energy Program, that Canada needs a tool-which is what Petro-Canada is-for the National Energy Program. They believe very strongly in their mandate and deserve a great deal more than some of the ill-conceived and somewhat despicable comments which come from the official opposition. They are attempting to do their job, they are doing it well, and I think Canadians all over the country, whether they be in the province of Newfoundland or in the province of British Columbia, are mindful of and respect the individuals associated with Petro-Canada for their great efforts.
Some members of the New Democratic Party indicated that one way to improve upon the activities of Petro-Canada was to have an enlarged board of directors which included individuals with various backgrounds, such as fishermen, environmentalists, sociologists, psychologists and others. I believe the individuals associated with Petro-Canada at the level of its board of directors are indeed very confident and are providing direction to that particular oil company. One individual who comes to mind is the president of the Newfoundland fishermen's association. He is a union man and a professional who is making a very worth while contribution to the direction of Petro-Canada.
Members of the official opposition have made many comments concerning the Canadianization aspect of the legislation, particularly in this amendment. I do not find anything wrong with the Government of Canada owning a piece of the oil and gas industry. I do not find anything overly distasteful about it. When I hear members of the official opposition saying that it is not a good thing, that it is wrong, or that we should not be doing it, I am tempted to ask them whether they would dismantle the Nova Scotia Power Corporation. Are they willing to speak with the Premier of the province of Nova Scotia, who belongs to the Conservative Party of Canada, and tell him that that Crown corporation is not needed? Would they destroy Nova Scotia Resources Limited, another provincial Crown corporation? Perhaps the argument could be written or spoken in such a way that if you are a Crown corporation you are okay as long as you are provincial; but if you are federal, somehow that ideology is wrong or no good.
Is Air Canada wrong? Is Canada Post, for which hon. members opposite voted, wrong? Conceptually, no; therefore the concept of Petro-Canada is not wrong either. They may have some difficulties with a particular program of a Crown corporation, and of course they should have an opportunity in which to voice their concerns. That is what the chamber is all about.
The Canadianization program and the energy legislation which is before the House are attempting to meet the needs of both the public and private sectors. We stated very clearly in the National Energy Program that the Government of Canada wanted to acquire more public ownership. I do not think there is any doubt on either side of the House that that intention was a serious one. Our intention to have more Canadian ownership in the private sector is also an intention about which I do not think there is any doubt on either side of the House. We are providing very rich incentives for people to become involved and to participate in the oil and gas industry in Canada. The petroleum incentives program is one which comes to mind. We will debate it a little later.
The opposition, particularly the Conservative Party of Canada, has made reference to Canadianization, public ownership and so on, but it was the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) who stated quite clearly that it was the thrust of his party to move on the front of Canadianization.
June 8, 1982

There seems to be a dichotomy over there. That is not new to hon. members who sit in the chamber, as I do, day after day and find some members of the Conservative Party for this, some for that, and indeed those who are for both views.
Reference was made to the fact that somehow the legislation contained in Bill C-103 was anti-American. That is the line which was picked up by the official opposition. I do not believe for one moment that it is anti-American. I believe, as other members on this side of the House believe, that it is pro-Canada. I do not find anything distasteful about being proCanadian. I can understand certain members of the Conservative Party taking exception to that particular concept. Perhaps it is because the Conservatives have a vested interest or are involved in so many ways with the multinationals. They do want to see any Canadian participating in the extremely vital oil and gas sector of the Canadian economy.
However, when they make speeches throughout Canada and suggest that somehow the National Energy Program is antiAmerican, that is false. The National Energy Program is proCanadian and I think Canadians are extremely proud of that ideal. I therefore wish to reject that comment and the views expressed by the Conservative Party of Canada.
As well, hon. members opposite stand in their place to say that the National Energy Program is the cause of the oil and gas industry's present difficulties. I suppose the opposition would like to be able to insulate the oil and gas industry from the conditions which exist in the world economy. If you are a Tory that thinking is logical, but I am not a Tory. I would never subscribe to a philosophy such as that. The economies of other countries in the world, whether France, Germany, the United States or Britain, are in difficulty. The fact cannot be avoided that the oil and gas industry is involved in those economies which have high interest rates, high unemployment and high inflation. It also must bear some of the burden. It is not true to suggest that the oil industry has sustained all its difficulties due to one particular program, the National Energy Program.
I do not believe that the members of the Conservative Party wish to present a scenario without providing all the facts. It is very clear that those members are perhaps prisoners of their own philosophy, as they were aptly described by the member for Vancouver Kingsway. Although the Conservatives are very right wing, it is ridiculous to suggest that the Canadian government should invent policies which would insulate the Canadian oil and gas industry. However, in view of the present situation in the world economy, of which Canada is a part, the government has taken some very serious steps to provide much needed cash flow, such as the reduction of the PGRT, for example, and to create incentives and exemptions to aid the small producers in the oil and gas industry in Canada.
There has also been an update to what many Canadians realize is a successful National Energy Program. I do not believe there is a member on our side who would say that the National Energy Program is the panacea to all the ills of the energy world. That has never been suggested by anyone.

Nevertheless, the fact must be taken into consideration that Canadians enjoy some of the lowest gasoline prices in the world, certainly lower than those in many other countries, including Italy, the United States and Great Britain. Gasoline in those countries is more expensive than here.
Members of the opposition will rise to say that is not true and make comparisons in various parts of Canada. In my own province of Nova Scotia the Conservative government introduced a 15-cent tax per gallon of gasoline in its budget. That is a provincial tax but, of course, the opposition would be content to persuade Canadians that it is the fault of the federal government. I believe it is very wrong to do that, and I hope they have the courage to say that the provincial governments are partially responsible as well for higher gasoline prices in some of those jurisdictions which I have mentioned.
While I would like to refer to a few further points in the National Energy Program, I will conclude by saying that the government will vote against this amendment. I urge all members on both sides of the House to vote against this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I will only take a few minutes. At the outset I will just say that anyone who brings up the subject of a 15-cent provincial tax, having told the voters that 18 cents is too much and now intending to stand up in the House later today to vote for an increase of 52 cents a gallon in two taxes alone, has a credibility problem that will not quit. Those members who fought an election over an 18-cent increase and who then propose a 52-cent increase are creating a credibility problem which they cannot overcome. It takes a great deal of gall to mention a 15-cent tax when we are dealing with a bill which has a 52-cent per gallon tax hidden in it.
Anyone who has common sense will know that the National Energy Program is a disaster. An update to this program was introduced last Monday evening when a $2 billion mistake was admitted. We indicated in the House that evening that the update was still a mistake. Since that time those who are knowledgeable in the oil and gas industry have judged that mistake. Oil stocks, which only fall when the climate is bad, have fallen 200 points. Of course, the reason for that decline is the update which was introduced by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). The dollar has also fallen.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Dingwall) asks us to appreciate the employees of Petro-Canada. I have many voters who are employees of Petro-Canada and I value them, their work and what they are attempting to do. It is those same employees who tell us the shortcomings of Petro-Canada and what should be done for it to become a strong and vibrant company.
The parliamentary secretary has a lot of gall to stand in the House and say that Petro-Canada is a success story because it has assets of over $6.5 billion and a profit of $63 million after cooking the books. Those same financial statements contain

June 8, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
deferred charges that are greater than the bottom line profit. Hidden in those books are several billions of dollars of interest payments which the taxpayers pay and the company does not. If Petro-Canada were an ordinary corporation competing in the private sector, its losses would be staggering and its bankruptcy would be assured.
We have a clear indication of that credibility gap if the parliamentary secretary can stand in the House and say that bankruptcy is a success story for a large oil company operating in Canada. To say that 18 cents is too much and then to vote for 52 cents is a clear-cut example of incredibility; but to say that we have a Canadian oil company success story when, in reality, it loses hundreds of millions of dollars and did so last year, is to defy logic. None of the other similar-sized companies has a financial picture that would give us that indication. It is only one. For him to compare that one with the Power Corporation is also to defy logic.
In Canada today young people who want to get work in the electrical industry know that they will be working for a Crown corporation. The odds are 95 per cent plus, because that is the nature of the electrical industry in Canada, for historical reasons. But if these young people take training in a university to work in the oil and gas industry, they could work anywhere in the world. The difficulty with a Crown corporation in the field of oil and gas is, in reality, the difficulty of competing worldwide for staff people of quality.
An oil company is a gamble. There is never any certitude that when a well is drilled there will be oil at the bottom of the hole. It is a gamble. It is like picking a horse at a race track. What the Liberals would have us believe, with the support of the New Democratic Party, the "Liberal Party West", is that young people fresh out of university have better judgment in picking where to drill the wells than people with 30 or 40 years of experience.
Oh, oh!
In essence, that is what Petro-Canada is all about.

speechtext: We are not proud.

I want people to imagine the following: that we take 10 per cent of the federal budget and gamble it in the
oil and gas industry. If we were to take 10 per cent of the federal budget and put it on a horse race, would we ask some young people fresh out of college which horse to bet on, or would we instead try to find someone with years and years of experience working at a race track, training and conditioning horses? Whose judgment would we trust? Would we trust the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to pick a horse in a horse race? What experience does he have?
At least he picked the right end!

What training does he have for proposing that tax? Yet we want to give billions and billions of dollars to that man to put on that horse race. I suggest to Your Honour that that is the flawed logic. If someone wants to bet on a horse race, he will gamble or pick a number at random and see if his luck is good, or he might get advice from people who are knowledgeable about horses and about that race, because one who follows the expert's advice has a better chance of winning.
Another example which comes to mind is this: would we want all the painting in Canada to be done by a Crown corporation? Would we stand up in this House and say that all painting businesses should be owned by the Government of Canada and that all of those who wanted to be painters should become employees of the Government of Canada? What nonsense! Crown corporations do not have the kind of record which suggests that the Government of Canada should be running a painting business. What we have in Canada is a system where many people own different painting businesses. There are many small entrepreneurs and if we are in the market to hire a painter, we have a choice. We may choose someone who charges a little less than someone else because he does just as good a job, but he has discovered a way to do it faster and therefore cheaper. But if the Government of Canada owned all the painting businesses, all the painters would be paid the same amount because the charges would be the same, and 50 per cent would go to administration and 50 per cent to the painter. It would cost us three or four times as much.
That is the logic of the Liberal government in relation to the Canadian ownership charge. It wants a tax which will continue forever so that it can buy out all the little guys and have one state-owned oil company which would charge what it darned well pleased, which would take half the money it earned and put it into administration or some other place and the consumers in this country would pay twice as much for half as much service.
If there is any integrity on the other side, the government must do one of two things. The heading of this section states Canadian ownership charge". In committee we inserted the word "public" but the Liberal members voted against it. We proposed the word "public" so that it would become "Canadian public ownership charge", because the clauses which followed clearly indicated that the government could use the money to buy property and shares and hold those in the name
June 8, 1982

of the government. So a correct title for the way in which the clause is written would be "Canadian public ownership charge"; but the Liberal Party voted that down. It did not want the honesty of that.
Therefore, today we propose an amendment which would state that when the government collects that $3 million a day, it would have to spend it on increasing Canadian ownership and would not be able to go out into the marketplace and compete with other Canadian companies, to buy out assets of other Canadian companies. All we are asking is that this huge amount of $3 million a day be dedicated to the purchase of non-Canadian companies so that they can become Canadian. If hon. members opposite do not go for that, then it should be clear to every Canadian in every part of the country that the Liberal Party believes in government ownership and does not give a darn for Canadian ownership. Voting against this amendment would clearly say that. The government believes in government ownership and in the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources owning, but the government does not believe in Canadian ownership. That is what a vote against this amendment would signify.

Mr. Speaker, this motion deals with another aspect of this Canadian ownership charge which should be put on the record because it is one more example of why one cannot trust this government and of how it does not keep its word and its promises. I do not know if any of the trained donkeys over there know it or not, but this Canadian ownership charge-
Petroleum Administration Act
Your ears are awfully long.

-does not go into the Consolidated Revenue Fund, it goes into a Canadian ownership account. The reason for that is very simple. It does not show up in the blue book, it is not part of the estimates, and it therefore does not show up as part of government spending. So the Liberals can stand there with straight faces and say; "Look at how we are controlling government expenditures. See?"
Through this tax, $1.5 billion is collected from Canadian consumers for actual government spending. It is being spent to buy Petrofina, but it never shows up in the accounts of Canada. That is in violation of the recommendations of the Lambert Commission, which the Liberal Party said it endorsed. It has either forgotten that commitment or it was not honest in the first instance. It is in violation of the recommendations of Auditors General over the last few years. It is in violation of promises made by Liberals about being honest and open with regard to government spending. Through this amendment we are attempting to bring a little integrity to that dishonest bunch of book manipulators.
We would like this report referred to the Public Accounts Committee, a non-partisan, all-party committee, so that it will have the capability of examining the account to ensure that the moneys were properly spent, that there was not an abuse or that the moneys were not used to reward members of the Liberal Party through purchasing of other shares, etc. That is all this amendment does. If the members of the Liberal Party are interested in honouring at least some of the minor promises they made in the past and living up to some of the policy statements they made with all solemnity and commitment, they will vote for this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 8 is a straightforward request for accountability of funds being collected by the government. One of the bases of parliamentary government that is generally accepted is that money collected by the government must be accounted for. Therfore, this kind of clause is necessary in order to have that kind of accountability.
I agree with the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) that this money which is spent should be allocated through some kind of estimates which are legislated. That is not always done in these cases or in the case of many federal Crown corporations. Therefore, anything that can be done to increase accountability of money collected by the government should be supported.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak briefly about the wisdom of allowing the Public Accounts Committee to examine this kind of expenditure. I put on the record at public accounts a scenario that is relevant to the decision whether or not to vote for this amendment.

June 8, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
When you turn an aspect of the market over to a bureaucracy, you increase the possibility of mistake in the marketplace. I put on the record a series of decisions which have been made in relation to the petroleum compensation charge. One of those is a provision which was exploited by Petrofina.
It is my information that Petrofina increased its bottom line profit through the exploitation of government subsidies by something in the neighbourhood of 25 per cent. At a later point in time, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) used the vehicle of Petro-Canada to purchase Petrofina. The consequence for the Canadian taxpayer was that one set of government subsidies inflated the selling price of a set of shares bought by the Canadian taxpayers through the energy minister. We have suggested in this House that the Canadian people paid about twice as much as they should have paid for the purchase of Petrofina. That is over $700 million too much which the taxpayers of this country had to pay. We inserted this amendment so that a body of Parliament, the Public Accounts Committee, would have the power and the authority to examine situations of that kind and recommend to Parliament and the government ways of avoiding $700 million mistakes in the future.
Regardless of ideology or party, Liberal and NDP members should see the wisdom of this Progressive Conservative amendment which simply says that a report which must be laid before Parliament should automatically be examined by one of the standing committees of Parliament. If we believe in the electoral process and in democracy and believe there is some point to Members of Parliament examining expenditures, then we must support this amendment.

He said: Mr. Speaker, originally this motion appeared in the name of the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes). I can understand the mistake because we are both similar in views and appearance.
This is a very simple motion. In this bill the government proposes to give itself the power to fix oil and gas prices unilaterally if necessary. speechtext: However, Mr. Speaker, I know what he is thinking of. He is thinking about the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) and the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre). Mr. Speaker, I want to speak in support of this amendment. I do not know why the government is afraid to give ten members the right to call for a debate in the House of Commons if and when they decide to undertake some new nationalization program and buy some oil company and impose this tax. Why do they insist on 30 members and think that ten is too small a number? It makes no sense, unless they are of the view that it is an intolerable imposition in the House of Commons that we should bring forward a motion requiring the government to explain why it is spending taxpayers' money. If they had any consideration for what this House is supposed to be, even in the most modest way, namely a forum to debate and discuss, they would accept this motion.
One could almost make a very good case that one member should have that right, but certainly ten members is not an onerous or unreasonable number. I am surprised and disappointed that the government has taken the view they have.
I would take this opportunity to point out that Clause 39 as amended in committee is a vast improvement over what the government originally proposed. Those people over there in the bowels of the bureaucracy who draft legislation are constantly seeking ways in which they can neuter this House as much as possible, because we are nothing but an imposition upon them as they pursue their good works on behalf of the nation. They produced an original procedure which had the ludicrous effect, Mr. Speaker, of meaning that the government could propose to buy a new oil company, the House of Commons could say no in a motion, but they could still go ahead and do it if they had the approval of the Senate. So you had the ludicrous situation where the House of Commons, made up of elected members of Parliament, could in the majority say no and we could not stop the government from acting; they could still go ahead and spend taxpayers' money.
That is an absolute affront to any reasonble interpretation of democracy. I suggest that whoever dreamed up that little scheme should be fired immediately and removed from the bureaucracy, because he is a danger. Apart from that, this is a violation of the Canadian Constitution because it has the effect of letting the Senate, an appointed body of has-beens, authorize the government to spend taxpayers' money. That is simply not tolerable in a democracy and I think it is in violation of our Constitution. The appointed people in the other place have no
Petroleum Administration Act
right to spend taxpayers' money; yet the original proposal from the government would have had that effect.
After considerable debate in the House, considerable debate in committee, and much more pressure than should have been necessary from our side, the government did make an amendment. And I give credit to the member for Etobicoke North (Mr. MacLaren) for taking that recommendation to the bureaucrats and saying "Try again". Ultimately they did, and we are pleased to see that change come about.
It is unfortunate that he did not spend a little more time with that bureaucrat or that collection of bureaucrats and convince them that it would have been quite reasonable to have ten members as the necessary minimum for triggering this mechanism, that 30 members is simply an attempt by the government to make it as difficult as possible ever to exercise this one, slim, minor, modest little check on government power.
I consider it unfortunate, regrettable and anti-democratic that the government is apparently going to vote against this amendment.

Motion No. 10
That Bill C-103, an Act to amend the Petroleum Administration Act and to enact provisions related thereto, be amended by deleting Clause 40.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this section is really a retroactive section. Earlier this day the former parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources mentioned that there had been a cutback in Alberta oil, western Canadian oil. In order to increase importation, the government collected an extra tax for a period of six months.

June 8, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
The House should be aware of two or three points regarding that tax. First of all, it was at 7.5 cents a gallon. The first thing we discovered in committee was that in six short months the government had collected more than $140 million too much. Even if one accepts the logic that a special tax is necessary, the rate of that tax was 40 per cent too high.
The only conclusion a rational human being can draw from that is that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) shamelessly used this chamber and his backbench members to make a political statement. He told Canadians it would cost them 7.5 cents a gallon more because of those cutbacks when in reality the extra amount, if there ever was one, would have been less than five cents a gallon. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources should be held accountable to this chamber for that tax.
Canadians may remember that in early September an agreement was reached and the cutbacks were stopped. A marvellous thing happened. That 7.5 cents a gallon tax did not disappear. The tax was there for a reason. The reason disappeared, but the tax of 7.5 cents a gallon stayed. What did the minister do? He simply increased another tax 7.5 cents a gallon the day this tax should have stopped.
Earlier today we warned Canadians that the 4.5 cents a gallon Canadian ownership charge is a tax, and last week and all day yesterday we warned Canadians that the 48 cents a gallon for the petroleum compensation fund is also a tax, which once they start this government intends to collect. We were telling the truth. The reality of that truth is here in Clause 40. The tax imposed is 40 per cent too high. It was for a specific purpose, but when the purpose stopped, the tax was simply transferred and it is still collected.
It was marvellous to listen to the testimony given in committee. We asked how the department calculated the need for this tax and were told that in Canada we require all refiners to estimate the amount of domestic crude they will use. When we were told that there would be so much cutback in the western provinces, we said to ourselves that we will have to import that much more and will have to pay extra for it. Production of Canadian crude was down, but imports did not increase because Canadians were learning to conserve. In effect, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and his officials had imposed a tax on conservation.
That is what this tax is. That is what this charge is all about. It is an extra price imposed because Canadians listened and started to conserve. They started to drive smaller cars. They insulated their homes. They began to discontinue using oil products and are using natural gas. Canadians did what their government said they should do. They cut down on the need to import oil. As a reward, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, supported by all his backbenchers, said: "We will tax you more. Do what we tell you is good, and we will tax you more". That is what Clause 40 is all about. It is a tax which
never was necessary. It was an inflated 40 per cent, and when the political excuse disappeared the tax stayed.
Then about 63 days later the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources blamed the oil companies for increasing prices. Is this a government in which Canadians are supposed to believe and have trust and confidence? It is a sham. This is a government with no shame. Its backbench has no shame. Hon. members opposite went out and told voters 18 cents was too much, but in this bill alone there is a 48 cents tax, a 4.5 cents tax and a 7.5 cents tax. Those are the taxes Canadians pay.
Then there is the export tax, which is the very first part of the bill. It was originally imposed on Canadians in 1974-75 because revenue was needed to pay for imports. In the last few years not one dime of it has been used to pay for imports. All that money goes into the federal treasury. We are taxed for a reason, and then when the reason disappears, the tax remains. That is the history of this government. That is the history of this Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and we have moved this amendment so that we will have the opportunity to point out with the greatest possible clarity that the tax was never necessary. It was imposed-at a rate 40 per cent too much-for a specific purpose, but when the purpose disappeared, the tax remained. Sixty-three days later the oil companies were blamed because prices went up.
If there is a Canadian tax revolt, it will be because of the behaviour of those who stand in this chamber and support this kind of principle and this kind of clause. It is onerous and deceitful, and we should make a statement in this chamber that as Members of Parliament elected by the people of Canada we do not support that kind of deceit in terms of the taxes which come out of our pockets.
