Motion No. 11
That Bill C-103, An Act to amend the Petroleum Administration Act and to enact provisions related thereto, be amended in Clause 42 by striking out line 9 at page 35 and substituting the following therefor:
"with the regulations provided that the amounts of such payments shall not cause the price of imported petroleum to a processor, that is the price that is effectively reduced after compensation, to fall to a level below the price of a comparable quality or kind of domestic petroleum."

Mr. Speaker, this amendment is an attempt to put some discipline into the ridiculous situation we have wherein we are subsidizing Mexican, Venezuelan and Arabian crude. Taxpayers are paying that subsidy to the point where foreign crude is cheaper than Canadian crude, the price of which is set by fiat. This is causing Canadian production to be shut in. It is causing cash flow problems for the exploration and production companies affected. It is causing business drop-offs for the oil service companies which would normally be servicing wells. It is causing a loss in royalties to the provincial governments affected. It is causing a loss of petroleum revenue taxes to the federal government. It is causing a loss to Canada in general of hundreds of millions of dollars.
A few years ago we in this country and in this House had a sense of outrage and indignation when the Canadian Egg Marketing Agency allowed some 28 million eggs to go rotten on the shelf. Members in this House and people generally were rightfully and justifiably angry and upset because an incompetent marketing board allowed that kind of waste. It was a waste of food and a waste of money.
That waste is insignificant compared with the waste which has been going on because of the way the petroleum import compensation program has been working. In the month of April 300,000 barrels of Canadian crude oil production were shut in daily. That meant we were importing the equivalent amount from Mexico, from Venezuela and from Saudi Arabia and subsidizing it to the tune of about $20 a barrel.
The taxpayers of Canada were paying $6 million per day in subsidies to Pemex, the Mexican oil company, and others, while 300,000 barrels per day of Canadian production was shut in. If that production had been in Quebec the roof would have lifted, Mr. Speaker. There would have been outrage, indignation and fury at that kind of treatment by the federal government. But the shut-in production was in western Canada, Saskatchewan and Alberta, so who cares? Some companies went bankrupt because they did not have any business, but who cares? It is not important. Who cares that the government is bungling the import compensation so badly? Nobody cares. It is taking place out there, so no one cares.
If the socialists needed an example of why the state should not be allowed to run anything they need look no further than this program. "Big Brother", the Liberal government with its high-priced officials, says in effect, "We have this brilliant scheme and we will administer it for the benefit of Canada." In the process the taxpayers of Canada pay $6 million per day
Petroleum Administration Act
in unnecessary taxes. That money ends up with Pemex, the Mexican petroleum company, and Petroleos de Venezuela, the Venezuelan state-owned company, or with a Saudi Arabian company. In the process, since we cannot afford $6 million per day, we have to borrow at 18, 19 or 20 per cent interest because there is a current account problem in the rest of the country. This contributes to our balance of payment problems. It is an incredibly stupid move, Mr. Speaker.
It is not as if the problem were a recent one. Last October the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was told about it but he did nothing until April when the action he took was not adequate. He said, "I will phone the refiners and ask them not to buy cheap oil on the spot market". That was his reaction to this insane situation that has existed at least since last October. If it were not so tragic it would be laughable.
One has to wonder what kind of gall it takes for the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Dingwall) to claim that the National Energy Program is a success. Would it be a real success if, instead of $6 million per day in unnecessary taxes, we were paying $12 million and if, instead of 300,000 barrels per day of shut-in oil, it was 600,000 barrels per day of shut-in oil that was affected?
I suppose all that would make it an outstanding success! The people responsible for operating the program in such an inept manner would resign if they had any decency, but that is not something we can expect from them.
We put forward this motion which, in effect, says that if you are going to operate an import compensation program, if you are going to subsidize Mexican oil-and heaven knows that is a stupid policy-but if that is what you insist upon doing, at least for goodness sake do not do it in a way that penalizes Canadian producers. That is a very reasonable request, and this is a reasonable motion. It asks that this program of subsidies to Mexico not be run in a way that will hurt Canadian producers.
It is ironic that most of the 300,000 barrels per day shut-in production comes from wholly Canadian-owned companies. It just turned out that the shut-in Canadian production came from fields dominated by Canadian companies. So, while the government is saying that the national energy policy will Canadianize the industry, it is subsidizing imports from Mexico, inflicting economic harm on the nation and, in particular, on Canadian-owned companies. Anyone with a shred of decency would blush, if not apologize, for supporting a government that would maintain and sustain that kind of absurd program.
While acknowledging that there is no likelihood that the trained donkeys will think any more independently about this motion than they have about others, nevertheless I plead with them to examine it, to examine their consciences, to live up to their responsibility as Members of Parliament, and support this reasonable amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I thought that a member of the government might speak and indicate

support for this motion. I am disappointed that such is not the case.
Canadians should understand that what the government has put in place is a system that works roughly in the following way. If the government were to put a tax of, say, $1,000 on every vehicle sold in Canada, and then all imported vehicles were to receive a subsidy of $5,000 so that they would be cheaper than a comparable Canadian made car, then under those circumstances Canadians could not be blamed for buying imported cars. But of course more people in the Canadian automobile industry would lose their jobs.
That is what the government has been doing in the oil and gas industry. Imported oil is more expensive than Canadian oil. It is all taxed, then the money collected is given over to the imported oil. When that $18 per barrel is given to the company that imports Mexican oil, all of a sudden, instead of being $9 more expensive than the Canadian it becomes $9 cheaper. Can a refinery be blamed for buying imported rather than Canadian oil under those circumstances?
Could the buyer of an imported car be blamed if our government made it cheaper than a comparable Canadian manufactured car? What about a toaster? Collect a tax on all toasters, Canadian or imported, and then give the money to the people who import toasters. Imported toasters will then become cheaper than the ones made in Canada, and Canadians will lose their jobs. That is what the government has been doing in the energy industry.
It is a peculiar fact of life, Mr. Speaker, that the current Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) himself directed PetroCan to buy 50,000 barrels per day of Mexican crude. That is the only purchase which the minister directed that company to make, and it is really strange that it is Mexican crude which benefits the most. It costs $9 more a barrel, but he set up a subsidy system which makes it $9 cheaper. If you went to the marketing area of the refinery in Quebec which uses that cheaper oil you would not find gasoline any cheaper. The subsidy makes it $9 a barrel cheaper, but the consumer does not find it any cheaper. The profits go into the pockets of the big oil companies. The minister takes tax dollars and turns around and subsidizes imported crude.
What we propose in this amendment, Mr. Speaker, does not go as far as I would like. I propose that we say to the minister he cannot use our tax dollars to make imported oil cheaper than domestic. You cannot take my taxes and reward the companies which import oil, and punish Canadian companies. You have to give Canadian companies an even break. That is all we are trying to do with this amendment.
Is there anyone with common sense who thinks it makes sense to put a tax on refrigerators, televisions, toasters or automobiles and then give it to the people who import those products so that they can sell at a price lower than the price of Canadian-made products? It defies common sense. Yet, somehow, members of this House continue to support a
minister who is doing just that with imported oil. It defies logic. All those Canadians on fixed incomes, all those Canadians who are having trouble paying the high cost of food or transportation, should know that the Liberal Party wants to make all those things more expensive so that it can take the money and give it to Mexico, Venezuela, and Saudi Arabia.
If we do not buy Canadian first, Mr. Speaker, then there will be fewer jobs for Canadians. The figures from last month show that has already happened in western Canada. Unemployment rates are going up rapidly. The government should remember that those unemployed people out there cannot buy trucks which are made in central Canada, or tires or toasters, all those things that are made in central Canada. That is what the government is doing, Mr. Speaker.
We simply ask that this Chamber, through this amendment, indicate to the Minister of Energy that he cannot use our tax dollars to provide a subsidy for foreign oil in order to make it cheaper than Canadian oil. If he really cared, he would go one step further and say it should always be a few cents more expensive per barrel so that there would be an incentive to buy the oil produced in Canada before we buy oil from other countries. That makes economic sense, helps reduce the cost of living, and will create jobs in Canada. We need all those things desperately, and this amendment would help to achieve them.

The Conservatives stood in this chamber and made reference to assistance for the oil and gas industry. The Government of Canada announced in its National Energy Program a specific item to assist, and it is here, in Bill C-104, but what did the Tories do? They walked off the job for two weeks, allowed the bells to ring, took their big salaries, and ran away from the House of Commons. But they had the nerve to say, through their literature and on television and in articles in the newspapers, that they were concerned and wanted to assist the oil and gas industry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Hypocrisy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
It is hypocrisy at its best. And who is it from? It is from the Conservative Party of Canada under the leadership of the Right Hon. Joseph Clark.
These incentives will encourage foreign-controlled companies willing to work with Canadians to develop Canada's oil and gas potential. Foreign-controlled and owned companies continue to be welcome to explore for oil and gas in Canada, despite the rhetoric that one hears from the Conservative Party of Canada. The prospective returns for such companies are competitive, if not superior, to similar investments in other western oil producing nations. Nevertheless, the degree of foreign control and ownership in this strategic sector of our resource economy must be reduced. The path the government has chosen is to stimulate Canadian private investment through a scheme of incentives for Canadianization. These incentives are to be given to Canadians participating in oil and gas exploration and development, in order to achieve a 50 per cent ownership of the oil and gas industry by 1990 and energy security for all Canadians. The legislative mechanism for the achievement of such goals is the bill before us today, Bill C-104.
There are three distinct parts to this bill, the first containing provisions for exploration and development incentives to be granted to Canadians in varying amounts according to their Canadian control status and degree of beneficial Canadian ownership. The provisions under which Canadian control and Canadian ownership will be determined are found under Part II. The aim of these provisions is to ensure that the incentives benefit Canadian-owned and controlled companies and that Canadian participation in exploration and development is encouraged.
Part III of the bill amends in a technical way two provisions of the Foreign Investment Review Act. The definitions of a non-eligible person and corporation are amended to reflect

June 8, 1982
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
policy that has been applied by the Foreign Investment Review Agency since the enactment of the FIRA Act in 1974.
Part I, entitled "The Petroleum Incentives Program Act", provides cash incentives to applicants who incur eligible exploration and development expenditures. Generally, the percentage of an incentive will depend on some or all of the following factors: first, the Canadian ownership rate of the applicant; second, the control status of the applicant, and, third, the type and location of the expenditure.
The bill provides for two incentives. The Crown share incentive amounts to 25 per cent of any eligible exploration expenditure incurred on Canada Lands. Entitlement to this incentive does not depend on the Canadian ownership rate or the control status of the applicant. The Crown share incentive will encourage and assist the exploration effort in Canada Lands, while contributing towards a share of such expenditures commensurate with the government's retained interest in the Canada Lands.
There are three higher levels of incentives, again representing a percentage of the eligible exploration or development expenditures or eligible asset costs incurred by an applicant.
Entitlement to this incentive is dependent on the applicant being Canadian controlled and having a minimum Canadian ownership rate of 50 per cent. The incentive levels as a percentage of eligible expenditures increase as the Canadian ownership rate of the applicant increases.
The rules for determining ownership and control status are found in Part II of the bill, entitled "The Canadian Ownership and Control Determination Act". A Canadian ownership rate is based upon beneficial ownership. This ownership determination may require looking through nominees to establish where the real beneficial ownership resides. As well, such measurement takes into consideration an investment in a chain of ownership. Beneficial ownership includes rights to equity in the future and to other forms of participation besides that of traditional equity. The control status determinations are made on the basis of control-in-fact. The Foreign Investment Review Act definitions and presumptions of control-in-fact will be used for such determinations.
Bill C-104 has been before the Standing Committee on Energy Legislation. A number of witnesses appeared before the committee to make submissions on the bill, including representatives from the Canadian Petroleum Association, the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada, the Canadian Bar Association, the Consumers' Association of Canada, and the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants. Individual companies appearing with submissions were Dome Petroleum Limited, Norcen Energy Resources Limited, Home Oil Company Limited, Gulf Canada Limited, Texaco Canada Resources Limited, and McLeod Young Weir Limited.
In committee witnesses addressed several issues. One issue raised by many of the submissions and the members of the committee was that there was no mechanism established within the bill by which an appeal could be made regarding an incentive or ownership decision. I am pleased to announce to the House on behalf of the Government of Canada that we
have considered these representations and that the bill will be amended so that the determination of a Canadian ownership rate under Clause 39(2), a redetermination of Canadian ownership rate under Clause 44(1), and a finding by the minister that an arrangement is artificial under Clause 30 and 53(1), are all now specifically subject to review by the Federal Court of Appeal.
This amendment will make the COR determination and redetermination as well as the PIP and COR artificial transactions divisions subject to review under Section 28 of the Federal Court Act. This amendment is a result of responsible government. We have a committee. Representations were made at the committee level by Members of Parliament, the industry and the academic community to improve this bill. The Government of Canada is attempting to do that. That is what that amendment is about.
Several other amendments were introduced in committee stage. While most of these amendments were technical, one amendment to Part II of the bill is worth noting specifically. This amendment would allow applicants who have begun to determine their Canadian ownership rate and control status on the basis of the draft forms and regulations, published on March 10, 1982, to rely on the provisions in those drafts for their COR.
Several other issues were addressed in committee. One such issue was that the provisions of the bill are complex. In the case of PIP, a key consideration has been the recognition that the benefits conferred by PIP on Canadians could, in a variety of ways, be transferred to non-Canadians. This has led to the adoption of rules to reduce such transfers to a minimum. However, while these rules introduce a complicating factor to the PIP system, they still allow for the self-assessing process to be applied and should be readily understood by those familiar with the terms and conditions commonly found in the wide range of industry agreements in use.
As for the Canadian ownership and control determination act, it is intended to measure real beneficial ownership. Sometimes this can be a relatively simple process, but for other cases it is more difficult. The COR system of rules for the measurement of Canadian ownership is designed to be applied as uniformly as possible to individuals, private and public corporations and partnerships, and many other investment vehicles such as trusts and insurance companies. The equity structure of each one of these types of entities is extremely varied and, of course, the COR rules must parallel them to be effective. It is in this sense that the rules are necessarily detailed.
The degree of ministerial discretion and the fact that many of the measurement and incentive rules are prescribed by regulation was another issue raised in committee. Because financial structures and oil and gas transactions are sensitive to change, it is considered desirable to retain a certain degree of flexibility in order for the government to be able to respond
June 8, 1982

to new and unforeseen situations. However, while these provisions are intended to ensure that the PIP and COR programs are responsive to industry needs and changing circumstances, I want to stress that the flexibility inherent to these programs is not intended to detract from, but rather to reinforce, the long-term nature of the PIP and COR programs. Indeed, the flexibility provided is by way of fine tuning to ensure that relief is provided in circumstances where the rules could otherwise lead to an arbitrary or an unintentionally hard result for PIP and COR applicants.
Another issue raised in committee was the fear that confidential industry information would be disclosed through these new programs. The confidentiality provisions in the statute permit disclosure of information to appropriate officials and departments for purposes of administration of the act, as well as to the Petroleum Monitoring Agency and the Department of Finance for purposes of monitoring the oil and gas industry and development of fiscal policies.
In addition, the statutory disclosure provisions recognize that the public interest in the administration of justice outweighs the public interest in the statutory protection of confidentiality in two circumstances. The first of these is any kind of legal proceedings, civil or criminal, arising out of the administration of the act in which evidence is to be taken under oath. The second of these is criminal proceedings of any kind. The ability to disclose in the latter circumstance reflects the position that when the important issue of criminal guilt, and perhaps the liberty of the subject is at stake, all relevant evidence might be available to ensure a proper resolution.
The officials have been instructed to keep in close touch with the industry to review the provisions of this bill for any changes that may be required. Any such changes will be considered within the context of the integrity of the program. The continuation of this dialogue is an extension of the effort that began with the inception of the program.
The specifics of the petroleum incentives program and the Canadian ownership rate and control status system were first set out in papers for public discussion in late 1980. These were further elaborated and refined in light of subsequent public comments in the spring of 1981. Public comments and reactions to both papers were reflected in the draft bill tabled in this House last June. The regulations for these programs have reflected this interaction with industry.
In addition, a series of workshops on both the PIP and the Canadian ownership and control determination programs took place earlier this year. Approximately 1,500 people attended these sessions in six different centres across the country.
Those attending came from both large and small companies active in the oil and gas sector as well as from the legal and accounting communities and from such financial institutions as banks, trust companies and investment dealers. Indeed, the key role to be played by the latter group has prompted separate follow-up sessions with them. Throughout the course of these and similar contacts, the exchange of information has contributed to both a better understanding and, we think, a more workable program.
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
In light of the extensive dialogue with industry and the support of the Canadian people across the country for the objectives of these programs, the Canadianization goal of the National Energy Program would appear to be a necessary component of a viable solution to this country's energy problems. Increased Canadian ownership and enhanced exploration activity will enable us to achieve our energy security and ownership goals and will also ensure that the benefits of industrial expansion are distributed more fairly across this country.
I am pleased to recommend this bill to the House as it will be instrumental in enabling us to resolve many of this country's energy problems. It will help this country become self-sufficient in energy by the end of the decade. It will help Canadians achieve control of the petroleum industry.
It is critical that these programs be put in place as soon as possible. There is an urgent need for the incentives by many Canadian oil and gas companies which believed in the National Energy Program and made investment decisions on the basis of the imminent availability of subsidies under the Petroleum Incentives Program. The Petroleum Incentives Program and the Canadian Ownership and Control Program will both play a vital role in securing our energy future.
As I said at the outset, if industry has one concern or, indeed, one complaint, it ought to direct it four-square to the Conservative Party of Canada. Never before have we seen such hypocrisy from a Canadian political party. For two weeks they goofed off. They left Parliament Hill. They had the bells ringing while important legislation like this Bill C-104 was delayed. This Bill C-104 has been delayed by their tactics. They referred to bankruptcies and to hard times in the oil and gas industry, but they did absolutely nothing about it when they had an opportunity. I hope they will have the courage to stand and say to the oil and gas industry and to the people of Canada that they made a mistake. They are used to making mistakes, whether it is in positions on Petro-Canada or something else. We have heard it all and we will hear it again, if they continue to make mistakes and blunders.
They have an energy policy to which they alluded today. It is in bits and pieces. One point is to dismantle Petro-Canada, to cut the prices of oil and gas. That is their policy. They say, "Never mind the agreement of the producing provinces." They never had what we refer to in my community as the guts, the intestinal fortitude, to take those policies before a policy convention of the Conservative Party of Canada and have them voted on in terms of resolutions. Not one resolution emanated from that policy conference.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: They were too scared.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
We know they are scared. They are scared that this energy legislation will do something for the oil and gas industry. Their intent is to see that industry go down the tube. I say to the Conservative Party: "Shame, shame, the

June 8, 1982
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
industry will make you accountable in the next general election."
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, it was interesting to hear that we "want the industry to go down the tubes". Would the parliamentary secretary go to Hamilton and see whether they are making tubes any more, or making pipe any more? Two years of this minister and they are not making any pipe, they are not making steel. That is Liberal policy.
In a court of law, in a criminal trial, one of the principles that all of us hold dear is that we cannot self-incriminate, we have the right to avoid self-incrimination. This Chamber is a marvellous place because so often members plead guilty and do not even know they have just done so. The parliamentary secretary stood and said that for two weeks the Conservative Party rang the bells and goofed off. Well, Mr. Speaker, the fact is that we spent those two weeks talking to the Canadian people about the reason why the bells were ringing. The people listened and they knew we were telling the truth.
Hear, hear!

They supported us then and they support us today. The parliamentary secretary starts there and he finishes there, saying that we were "goofing off while the bells rang." In the middle, Mr. Speaker, comes his guilty plea. He puts it out there for all of us, with pride. Mr. Speaker, do you remember him saying to you and to all the members of this Chamber: "We have changed the legislation; when we listened to the witnesses, we learned; we have put before you tonight 12 amendments, we had a whole lot more in committee."
The bells rang, Mr. Speaker, because the Liberal government was not going to let the bill go to committee, the bells rang because the Liberal government was not going to hear witnesses. Now they stand in this Chamber and admit to the nation that they have 12 amendments tonight and had a whole bunch more in committee. That, Mr. Speaker, is because witnesses were heard, because the government learned. It is a rotten bill, but it is better, and it is only better because the bells rang for two weeks.
Right on.

I love to stand in this Chamber and point out that the parliamentary secretary has been admitting that those bells rang for a reason. The reason was so that knowledgeable Canadians could be heard, that legislation could be changed, and that it might be made a little bit better. He stood up there and he told us that all those things happened, that Canadians were heard, and that he is proud because the bill is going to be better. And the proof is in the order paper today: 12 amendments that we debate this evening and perhaps tomorrow, and then we go to vote on them. None of those amendments, Mr. Speaker, would have been available for Members of Parliament to vote on if the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), the House leader and the backbenchers of the Liberal Party had had their way and had rammed this bill through, without witnesses.
What are they so proud of? Do you know what we have here in this package of bills and in this one in particular? In the package we have all kinds of ways of taking money out of the pockets of the consumers and out of the corporations which employ people, the corporations that buy steel and trucks and so on. We take it all away from them and then we get to Bill C-104 and we give it back, not all of it but part of it.
Mr. Speaker, do we give it back to those who have earned it, who have the knowledge to use it rightly? Do we do that in this piece of legislation? No, we do not, Mr. Speaker, we give it back to whomever the minister of energy decides shall get it, whether they know anything, whether they earned it, whether they are going to use it wisely, whether it will add one drop of oil. No, those are not the criteria, Mr. Speaker. The criterion is that the minister of energy shall decide who gets it. Is that wise for Canadian consumers?
Just stop to think about it for a minute. In the city of Ottawa today we have a lot of grocery stores. Some of them do a good job, bringing into their stores the things that people want. They charge a reasonable amount so that they can keep their good employees, and they stay in business. Others do not do so well. They buy the wrong groceries, they put them on the wrong shelves, they do not display them well, people do not buy, and they go out of business. What does that system produce? It produces for us all a system of pretty good grocery stores, because if the manager is bad, he is going to fail; if the store is well run, it will succeed.
Do we apply that logic to the oil industry? No, we do not. We say, "If you are successful, if you find a lot of oil, we will take most of it away from you in the form of taxes." Then we add: "Are we going to give it back to you, because we know that you can do a good job of finding us more oil? No, we are not, we are going to give it back to whomever the minister of energy decides to give it back to." Do they have to have any experience in the oil and gas industry? No. Do they have to have ever drilled a well? No. That is not why they get some of this money back. Could you drill wherever you want, wherever your mind and your experience tells you you are going to find oil? The answer is no. You drill where the government tells you to drill. And you will get money for doing it if he decides you should get it. It has no relationship to experience, it has no relationship to where oil is likely to be.
We have seen some evidence of this. Where is he telling us in this legislation that most of the money is going to go? I will tell you. It will go to wherever it will cost the most. He is going to encourage everyone out there to drill in the most costly places, so that gasoline and oil to heat your house and drive your car will cost the largest amount possible. He will finance it by raising taxes. And somehow he has forgotten that for less cost you can produce gas and oil for people at a lower price. That was the system we had in this country until two years ago, but now the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Dingwall) stands in the House and brags that his government is going to take money
June 8, 1982

away from successful people and give it to an unknown bunch, but only if they drill in the most expensive places possible. If they find any natural gas or oil, it will cost consumers the maximum amount. It will cost them as much as possible. The government is doing everything it can in this legislation to raise the prices which must be paid to heat homes and drive cars. The parliamentary secretary has the gall to stand in this chamber and brag about that.
Let us think about what it would be like if the government took a little less and left all those companies-there were thousands-to make the individual decisions they had been making. Those companies were asking, "Should we drill here or should we drill over there?" Those companies made those decisions after 10 years, 20 years, 30 years or 40 years of experience, and they used their own money. They decided where they were most likely to find oil and gas, and the parliamentary secretary wants to replace that system with a system whereby a bureaucracy will decide where they should drill.
We were told in the committee that it will take 400 more civil servants to give money back. Who will pay for that? The senior citizens of Canada who are heating their homes will pay for those 400 more civil servants. The minister admitted that, and if his past projections are any indication of the future, that 400 will become 800 or 1,200, and their sole job in life will be to give money back. If we have to have 400, 800 or 1,200 to give it back, I suppose hidden behind are another 400 who had to take it away in the first place. Then, of course, we forget about the 1,200 or 2,400 who work in all the companies and who have to do the book work to decide how much is to be taken away. Then there is another group in each company which has to decide how much is coming back.
What have we done? If we have all those people employed in companies deciding how much is taken away and another group deciding how much is coming back, and if we have government employees who have to work to take it away and another group who have to work to give it back, what will happen to oil and gas prices? None of those people were necessary two years ago, but we are making them necessary. The people who will have to pay will be those people on fixed incomes, on pensions and on unemployment insurance. They are the people who will have to pay for this mess. We have done this to our system; now we tell companies where to drill, not because there is any oil there and not because it is the most likely place to find it but simply because the government wants the drilling to occur in some places rather than in others.
If a person has a summer cottage or a farm and he wants to drill to get some fresh water, will he just drill any old place, or will he seek a little help to find the best place to drill? It is expensive to drill a hole only to find out there is no water. That person will want to drill where he is likely to find water. The same is true in the case of oil. It is very expensive to drill a hole if no oil is found. A company will want to drill in the most likely place.
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
This legislation deserves the unanimous condemnation of all members of this House because it is based on the principle that big brother knows best where to drill. It is based on the principle that big brother has already decided that where companies will drill will be the most expensive places. Big brother has decided that the cost of gas and oil three years, four years and five years down the road will be incredibly high because big brother is forcing the industry to drill in those expensive places.
The parliamentary secretary stood in the House and said that the program is working because Canadian ownership is increasing. I would like to ask the parliamentary secretary whether he owns his own home. Does he own his own home, or does a mortgage company own his home? There is quite a difference between owning a home which is paid for and having a mortgaged home. Interest rates have doubled. People who thought they owned their homes suddenly found they did not own their homes when interest rates doubled, and they are going to lose their homes. The National Energy Program has encouraged Canadian companies to go out and borrow a lot of money to buy other companies. I will give one example. Dome is the biggest of Canadian-owned companies. A couple of years ago about half the money Dome was taking in was used to pay interest on money borrowed, but the other half was used for drilling, expansion, pipeline construction and development. As of about three weeks ago 90 per cent of the money which accrued to Dome was used to pay interest. Since that period two or three weeks ago interest rates have gone up, and the value of the Canadian dollar has gone down. The Canadian dollar closed today at 79.25 cents U.S. My suspicion is that that Canadian company does not have enough money coming in every day to pay for the money it borrowed. If it does not have enough money coming in every day to pay for the money it borrowed, it is bankrupt.
If the company goes bankrupt, who owns it? At first blush one might think it is a Canadian bank because Dome borrowed from a Canadian bank. However, we find that the Canadian bank borrowed from a foreign bank, and the real owner of Dome Petroleum is not Canadian. The ownership certificate says Canadian, but in reality when Dome borrows that much money, it is the people who lent Dome the money who own Dome, and those people are not Canadian. The parliamentary secretary would have us believe this program has produced more Canadian ownership. It has not. It has produced more Canadian borrowing.
Let us examine what borrowing does. If half the money Dome had was being used to build pipelines or drill wells in Canada, that half was being taxed. It was producing income. People were employed, and they paid income taxes. Cars were bought, and taxes were paid. However, when all the money Dome gets is used to pay interest and the ultimate borrower is a foreign bank, all the money consumers pay for oil and gas bought from Dome leaves the country and is not taxed because it is a business expense. No jobs are created, and no federal revenue is generated.

Petroleum Incentives Program Act
That is what the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has done to this country. Billions and billions of dollars have left the country in this way. The truth is that in the marketplace stocks are down, down, down because they are worthless. The truth is that the value of the Canadian dollar is down, down, down because it is becoming worthless. The truth is that one and a quarter million Canadians are unemployed today because there are no jobs. There is no money to drill wells, to buy cars, to buy trucks, to buy steel or to buy pipe because hon. members opposite blindly follow the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The minister is wrong. He has pride and pizzazz, but he is stupid. What he has done to this nation is a tragedy. Never in the history of this nation has there been a member of the cabinet who has done so much damage to the fabric of our country in such a short period of time. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is an absolute catastrophe. To vote for this legislation, in whole or in part, is to aid and abet a crime. It is a crime which approaches treason for what it has done to this country and what it will do in the future.
A few days ago the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) appeared at the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare. The topic was urea formaldehyde foam insulation, which the government had said was suitable for homes. It gave grants for its installation but later said that it was not healthy. Now people cannot sell their homes. For some the hope of retirement has been wiped out and others have lost their health. What was really disturbing was that when a group of those home owners came to ask the government for help the minister complained, saying the government had given them $60,000 to organize and therefore they had no right to criticize the government. So for $60,000 apparently we give up the freedom of speech!
That is what grants do, Mr. Speaker, they make people afraid to speak up. If the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) is going to hand out grants to people in the oil industry, will they have the courage to tell Canadians what is right and what is wrong? Freedom of speech is for sale, apparently. That is one of the cardinal principles of this minister and of many ministers on the front bench-that they can buy silence.
Bill C-104 which we are discussing tonight gives money to oil companies and in this way the government hopes for increased silence from the industry. There is a threat in this. Once you take the paycheque from the government you had better not criticize, because it can quietly cut you off. The most recent example of this was the civil servant, Neil Fraser, who worked in the tax department. He wanted to speak publicly about the dangers he saw in Canadian society, but he drew a paycheque from the government so it fired him.
The government now wants the whole oil industry to take a paycheque in the belief that once it is on the payroll, it will not be so critical. I have lived all my life around people in the industry, Mr. Speaker, although I have never worked in it. They are a rugged bunch of individualists, well trained and
with a lot of pride. They would be just as happy if this legislation were scrapped. But the minister and the parliamentary secretary do not understand that. People in the industry understand the danger to their freedom of speech and freedom of action which is inherent in the legislation. It tells people where to drill and when to drill. If they have any knowledge or experience they know that this legislation is one of the rotten elements in the whole package that will help drag everyone in the nation into increased dependency on foreign oil, a devalued dollar, higher inflation and increased unemployment. They feel as strongly about it in a negative sense as I do and I urge all members of the chamber to vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who just spoke said he lived all his life around the industry. As I listened to him I thought that I lived all my life during the course of his speech, which went from urea formaldehyde to civil servants and finally back to the oil industry.
We are supposed to be speaking to the first amendment, but it looks as if we are speaking to the whole bill. I want to say to the parliamentary secretary that I would like to look more closely at his speech tomorrow in Hansard because he announced some changes that may be significant. I should like to deal with them when we get to the clauses in question. The parliamentary secretary spoke about Conservative hypocrisy in this case. Talk about the pot calling the kettle black when you consider that the government was forced to listen to Parliament and divide the bill! That is the problem the government has with the people-the people do not think that it is listening. This is not a democracy but an autocracy, a government run by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and very few others.
It was good for the government to be forced to divide the bill. 1 am not sure that it lost much in the long run as the bills will be through the House within a couple of days. In any case, the government did have to eat crow. That is why we supported the division of the bill. It reminds me of the line in Macbeth about the bell- " ... it is a knell that summons thee to heaven or to hell". We are not sure whether the government will go to heaven or the other place yet. We will have to wait and see.
I want to say something about the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes). Talk about hypocrisy! The hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) wrote to the minister telling him to divide the bill and he might do better with the PIP grants because the industry wanted them. But tonight that party claims it is bleeding for the old age pensioners who will have to pay for all this. That is too much, Mr. Speaker, after they have spoken for about 12 hours putting forward the line of the industry almost exclusively. A brief presented by the Consumers' Association of Canada had this to say:
Bill C-104 and the philosophy behind it perpetuate the failed energy policies of the past-namely that future oil security can be brought through higher prices and subsidies for oil companies.
Last week the minister announced that $8.9 billion would be spent in PIP grants. That is a lot of money. It means that 80
June 8, 1982

cents of every dollar invested in exploration in Canada lands in the north and in the offshore will be borne by the taxpayers of Canada, and there will be another 13 cents in the dollar if it is a Canadian company paying taxes. That is 93 cents on every dollar, Mr. Speaker. It is no wonder that consumers feel they have a stake in this. The brief continues:
What should be kept in mind is that for every $1.00 increase in the wellhead price of oil and an equivalent rise in the price of natural gas, the consumer will pay industry and government $18,000,000,000 in higher prices for existing reserves of oil and gas, because the established volume of hydrocarbon reserves the industry says now remain in the conventional producing areas total the equivalent of 18 billion barrels of oil. With price hikes in excess of $35.00 per barrel in prospect by 1986, in this zero sum game the financial burden on the consuming sector of the economy will likely become unbearable, amounting, as it will, to hundreds of billions of hard-earned dollars in extra payments to the petroleum industry and to governments. The stakes are immense. That is why we see full page newspaper advertisements and multimillion dollar television campaigns sponsored by the petroleum industry.
I say to the consumers of Canada-do not be fooled; you are being hosed. You will have to pay $8.9 billion in petroleum grants and pay more at the pumps. You are dealing with two parties who want to give this money away. This money comes out of the pockets of consumers, Mr. Speaker, and goes into the pocket of the government and the pockets of the oil companies. If companies want to explore, I have no objection; but why do we have to give them $8.9 billion in grants? We are going to introduce amendments to this bill in which we tried to give the consumers in Canada a break, and give native people a chance to participate in the administration of these grants. We try to make sure that the required Canadian content is real and substantial. Those are the kind of amendments we propose, and I reserve my right to speak on the amendments of the parliamentary secretary.
This bill will give the big oil companies a lot of money, eight billion, in fact almost nine billion dollars, to be taken out of the consumer's pockets and put into those of the oil companies. This is incredible, at a time when families are having trouble paying their oil, gas and hydro bills. This legislation is far too generous to the big oil companies.

Therefore we will be making some amendments to the bill.

Mr. Speaker, the COR program and PIP grants, which are the substance of Bill C-104, are going to last maybe two years and then collapse. The reason for that was exemplified in the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). He clearly gave one of the reasons these programs will not survive. When the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) turned loose those little beavers in his department to work on this thing, these people with brilliant academic credentials and no knowledge whatsoever of the oil industry, they produced this little gem as a way of Canadianizing. They were going to get at the cash flows of the big companies throught the PGRT
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
and the NGGLT, these massive taxes, and recycle the money to Canadian-owned companies by way of PIP grants.
It was a great academic theory, the only problem is that the world is populated by more than just the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. The hon. member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre) raised the same questions in committee. These huge taxes have suddenly become the property of the government, and the grants are gifts from the people to the oil industry. They forget about the other part of the question and they say "What is going on? How can you give these billions of dollars to the oil industry when hospitals are closing and universities need money?" It is that kind of simple-minded reasoning which will dominate. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway quoted from the Toronto Star and reporters from that paper are going to repeat it ad nauseam. You can bet that anyone in this House with a cause will say "just a minute, you cannot say you do not have any money because you are giving these billions of dollars to the oil industry".
Right.

You see, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) forgets the other part of the equation. As socialists, of course, they believe first and foremost that all earned income belongs to the government. Anything left in the hands of the person who earned it represents a gift from the government to that person. Unfortunately that simple-minded approach is going to be adopted and accepted by others who will forget about the other part of the equation.
A second reason this program will die is that it is incredibly complex. The academics sat down and said we will have a grant system based on the degree of Canadian ownership. The more Canadian owned you are, the bigger the grant, and in that way we will be promoting Canadian ownership. That sounds marvellous on the back of an envelope but, as one of our representatives to the committee pointed out, consider a major trust company or insurance company. The majority owners are Scottish, and they in turn manage a pension fund whose major beneficiaries are Canadian, who in turn own stock in the company. Is the company Canadian? Is it British? Who knows? How do you trace the ownership? Well, the only way to keep track of it is to write regulations, so the beavers have been at work writing regulations. They have something like 60 pages of regulations and you have to be a Philadelphia lawyer to understand them. Mr. Speaker, when a member of a large firm of chartered accountants says that he and his partners have been examining the regulations and applications forms for some months-they are in Calgary and expect some of their customers will be interested-and they do not yet feel confident of their ability properly to advise clients on filling out these forms, what hope is there for the small Canadian-owned company which does not have on its staff the lawyers and accountants necessary?
The government has been holding seminars around the country on these programs and I have talked to several people who have attended them. I have yet to find a single person who came out of there and said anything but, "I haven't a clue

June 8, 1982
Petroleum Incentives Program Act
about how we are going to be able to operate that thing". Remember, it is not just the person applying for the grant who has to be concerned about it. The business world is complex, shares are held in the hands of individuals, banks, stockbrokers, and trust and insurance companies. There is a myriad of ways in which capital stock is held, and there is a myriad of instruments. A lot of companies will have common stock "A", "B", "C", preferred "A", "B", and so on. Stocks can be preferred or deferred in this way and that way. Some have dividends, some do not. There are all kinds of different instruments, Mr. Speaker, held in all kinds of different ways. To find out what percentage of your shares are owned and controlled by Canadians represents an incredibly complex activity. Application forms have to be sent to trust companies and stockbrokers saying, "You have a bunch of our stock in your name that you are holding for another beneficiary. Can you tell us whether that beneficiary is Canadian?" The broker answers by saying, "The beneficiary for this stock is 107652 corporation limited." The address shown is usually a post office box or a lawyer's office. The next thing you have to do is to go to the registered headquarters of 107652 limited to find out who owns that company. You may find the shareholders of that company are 10769 corporation limited, and so on.
It is amazing how complicated business is.

The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway says it is amazing how complicated business is. That is not what is amazing. What is amazing is how simple-minded some people can be about programs which they design on the back of envelopes.
This program does not have a hope of surviving that complexity. It is not in existence yet, but already there are in the order of some 400 civil servants trying to deal with it. Witnesses who have appeared before the committee have told us that the cost of administering this program within their companies will be in the order of a half a million dollars a year extra in non-productive, wasted administrative effort. That is for the companies with a vested interest. The banks have no vested interest in this program but they are going to have to deal with it. What is the incentive for them to deal with it? As a company, how are you going to get a bank, a trust company or a stockbroker to supply you with the information to fill out the forms? You will have to pay them somehow for that task. Who knows what those costs will be? What we do know is that the costs will be high. But we do know it is a totally wasted expenditure. It will not bring about one extra barrel of oil nor will it bring about one extra cubic foot of gas. It is a totally non-productive expenditure which will contribute to the continuing deterioration of productivity in this country.
It is a source of incredible frustration for me how little the government pays attention to its own policies. We have heard past Liberal governments say, this one did too-it is usually presidents of the treasury board who make the statements that they are committed to deregulation-that they are committed
to reducing the paperwork burden and to cutting red tape. We are told the Liberal government recognizes that red tape and bureaucracy lead to excessive bureaucratic influence through regulations, etc., and this leads to a deterioration in productivity. That is the Liberal government's policy. It has been stated repeatedly. Indeed, the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) set up an office called the Office for the Reduction of Paperwork Burden. What a fancy title. On the other hand, another government department, in this case the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, has guys sitting down designing the most incredible bureaucratic complex paperwork burden program that you can imagine. They are doing it without even a genuflection to what is supposed to be government policy.
This program will generate a lot of temporary jobs- because the program is going to collapse-for lawyers, accountants and paper shufflers. But none of this will contribute a barrel of oil or a cubic foot of gas. None of it will make us energy self-sufficient, but it will be good for the paper makers and for filing cabinet makers. There will be a ton of application forms and paper floating around from people who are trying to get information. It is the most complex program imaginable. How did it come about? A writer for Maclean's magazine was right. It was a minister who said, "Look, I have been a minister for a number of years and I have accomplished nothing. We are going to accomplish something now. Go out and design a program that will Canadianize the gas and oil industry." The minister turned loose all those bright young fellows with their Ph.D. degrees. They sat down in splendid isolation from the real world and they came up with this program.
One wonders how long it takes to learn something. In the energy pricing agreement of September, 1981, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said that the government was going to bring us export permits for Canadian-owned companies. In other words, the Canadian-owned companies would get first preference on the export of natural gas. What a marvellous theory. This was a marvellous theory to help Canadian companies. But a junior land man in the oil industry, fresh out of high school, could have told the minister and any one of his minions that was impossible. There is not a man alive or a team of lawyers alive who could tell you the nationality of a cubic foot of gas in less than about six months of continuous effort. It just is not possible. It is just so shockingly naive and stupid that you despair. You despair at that kind of naivete and stupidity that there is this continuing confidence that the government can do things right. The government cannot do it right. It has never been able to and it will not be able to do so in the future. This whole thing is going to collapse.
I understand the parliamentary secretary in his remarks muttered something about the ringing of the bells having been wasteful or something. I have gone over the history, but apparently there are modern attempts to distort history. But let us make things quite clear as to what happened with respect to the Energy Security Act and with regard to this program.
June 8, 1982

Last fall I approached the then parliamentary secretary to the minister of energy, mines and resources and said "Look, the junior oil companies are hurting badly and they need a shot in the arm. The only thing you have is this PIP and COR programs. Take that out of the energy security act and we will give it reasonably expeditious treatment, even though it is a dumb program and we don't like it, but if that is the way you are going to go, at least go that way. About 15 months ago 1 know of at least one company that approached the government and said "When is PIP going to come into force? We need it for our exploration program." The company was told that it would be out in May 1981. On the strength of that commitment by the government, it borrowed money, undertook an exploration program and, of course, was severely strapped.
The then parliamentary secretary said that he thought it was a reasonable suggestion and that he would talk to the minister. The minister returned and said that he would split it if we agreed to pass quickly the rest of the bill in one lump. I found that absurd. I had made an offer which I thought would be of assistance to the government, and the minister said that he would let us be of help if we would take the rest of the bill in one lump. It was similar to offering to sweep a neighbour's sidewalk, and he says, "Fine, you can sweep my sidewalk and my driveway as well". Obviously I said no.
Then I wrote a letter to the minister in December making the offer again. He wrote back in January and gave me a flat no. Then we know what happened in terms of the point of order I raised asking that the bill be declared inadmissible. Madam Speaker ruled that the bill could not be split, although I did not ask her to do that. Nonetheless, we were at the end of our tether and had no choice but to ring the bells until the bill was split.
What has happened as a result of the bill being split? We have had the opportunity to have committee hearings and to hear witnesses. I do not know how many witnesses there were, but it was in the order of 25 or 30 who would otherwise not have had an opportunity to present their views, had the energy security act gone through as was intended initially by the government. On Bill C-104 alone there were something like 1 5 amendments as a result of committee work. This would not have happened if we had not stuck to our guns and demanded that that atrocious piece of legislation be split before it was brought into the House of Commons.
As a result of sticking to our guns, Canadians had an opportunity to examine these bills closer, and on Bill C-104 there were some 15 changes, which means that some 15 mistakes would have gone through had the government had its way and brought in that one massive piece of legislation. We have not counted the total number of amendments to all bills, but a bunch of them were brought about as a result of our efforts to force the government to treat the House with a reasonable amount of respect.
When hon. members of the New Democratic Party say that we did a terrible thing by ringing the bells and forcing the
Petroleum Administration Act
government to break up the legislation, and when hon. members of the Liberal Party say that it was terrible for us to do these things, I say nonsense. It is one of the best things we have done in the last year, because it forced the bill to be broken up in a way that it could be handled by a committee of the House and because it resulted in amendments or improvements to the bill, albeit it is still a piece of trash.

Oh, oh!
