speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) has the floor.
Mr. Speaker-
Hear, hear!

-I appreciate your attempts to still the braying of the asses in the government ranks. They appear now to be somewhat still.
This bill is the bill which incorporates and puts into legislation the nefarious treachery of the government opposite with respect to oil and energy prices in this country. This is the bill that permits the government to raise the prices of oil and gas in this country, as the government has done 16 times since February of 1980.
Shame.

Twelve of those increases have been increases in federal taxes on oil and gas and all the products made from a barrel of oil. The increases total not 18 cents, not 20 cents,
June 8, 1982

not 24 cents, not 9 cents, not 38 cents, not 40 cents, not 42 cents, but 62 cents a gallon. The government has raised the prices and taxes paid by the people of Canada by that much not only on gasoline and diesel fuel but also on heating oil and every product made from crude oil. But, Madam Speaker- Mr. Speaker; sometimes I get confused-
Sometimes?

-about who is the chair. 1 will not deal tonight with the sins of this government in the field of energy pricing. I will deal with its attempt to wreck the confederation of our country and to oppress the people of Newfoundland and Labrador with its attitude toward the question of offshore mineral resources. I intend to deal with the conduct of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien)-who has so disgraced himself as the head of the system of justice of this country in this House in the last several weeks-in this connection. I will show how the minister attempted to misrepresent certain facts to the people in this House. I do not want to be interrupted, so I will not say whether it was intentional or not intentional. I will also expand on how the minister attempted to mislead the House of Commons Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs with reference to the precedents in this matter and how the government leader in the Senate attempted to mislead the Senators in the other House. Those innocents are not used to being misled, but the leader of the government in the Senate did the same thing.
If I can have a little silence from hon. gentlemen opposite, if the wind will stop blowing through their heads and out their mouths-they have a lot of empty spaces in their craniums- and if they will listen, I will show them how the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, the province of Nova Scotia, the province of Prince Edward Island, the province of New Brunswick, the province of British Columbia and all provinces which have shores and shelves lying off their shores have been betrayed by this government.
1 want first to deal with my own province, Newfoundland. If Newfoundland and Labrador had not entered confederation on March 31, 1949, there would be no question as to who owns the oil and gas which has now been discovered on the continental shelf off Newfoundland, the Hibernia field. It would clearly belong to Newfoundland under international law. There would be no question about who had control over the continental shelf and the 200-mile economic zone with respect to fisheries, because 66.66 per cent of the whole east coast, the continental shelf area, was brought into confederation by the Province of Newfoundland. That is the province that for 400 years had to struggle to exist and that today is still not economically selfsufficient. It brought all those resources when it joined confederation.
There is not one word in the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada that says the Province of Newfoundland should surrender its resources onshore or offshore to the Government of Canada. That was 1949 and not too much was
Petroleum Administration Act
known about the offshore resources in those days. A lot more is known today.
For 23 years after confederation there was a Liberal government in Newfoundland; a government that did not care whether Newfoundland ever became self-sufficient. It was satisfied just to be the trained seal in Newfoundland and then, if the Newfoundlanders voted the Liberal way they could come to Ottawa and the government would reward them with the largesse collected from all the people of Canada. That is if we were subservient and dipped our hats to them and were properly polite and swallowed our pride, they would see that we did not starve. That was the attitude of that provincial government in Newfoundland led by the first premier, Mr. Smallwood. It did not care about the offshore. It did now know about the offshore until 1960.
If that Liberal government had thought it had any title to the offshore, it could have been dangerous. It delivered all the rights to the offshore to Mr. John C. Doyle who, as we have seen in recent months, is being investigated by the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. He was given the rights to huge areas of the offshore by his friend Mr. Smallwood. The rest of the offshore was given to Mr. John Shaheen, late of the Come By Chance oil refinery who is now in some difficulty in the United States. In other words, two adventurers, two plunderers, two buccaneers, two close associates of the then premier of Newfoundland were given the rights to most of the offshore.
In 1972 a new government took office in Newfoundland under Premier Frank Moores, of which I am proud to have been a member. It appointed a young, intelligent, idealistic Newfoundland lawyer to head the Department of Mines and Energy in the person of Leo Barry, now a member of the Newfoundland House of Assembly. Within 12 months he had the situation under control and had cancelled all the permits given to Shaheen and Doyle and the political plunderers associated with the Liberal Party of Newfoundland.
The position taken by that first Liberal government of Newfoundland which agreed with the Government of Canada that it would be delighted to have 50 per cent of the revenues from the offshore, if there were any, went out the window. The new, Conservative government of Newfoundland decided that the resources were to be developed for the people of Newfoundland and that it would put forward a case for the Province of Newfoundland and let the chips fall where they may. If Newfoundland had any future, it could only come from the wealth that would be generated in the oil and gas it felt sure was off the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador.
We immediately repudiated the negotiations that had gone on between the Atlantic provinces and Newfoundland and the Liberal governments of Canada. We said that we were not going to surrender our one chance for economic self-sufficiency. Never. For 400 years tens of thousands of Newfoundlanders had to leave their homes and go abroad to work. They used to go to Boston, New York, all through the United States and all over the world. Now they are going all through Canada looking for work. We said that we aim for the time when the

June 8, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
man or woman born in Newfoundland will be able to stay and work in Newfoundland if they want to-and their children and their children's children. This is their only hope.
From 1972 forward that was the theme, the raison d'etre of the Newfoundland government-that and the development of the hydro resources in Labrador. We have been thwarted in the development of those hydro resources in Labrador but I will not go into that tonight. For reasons known to people who have been associated with the Liberal Party of Quebec and successive governments in Quebec, we have not been able to develop our hydro resources in Labrador.
When Mr. Smallwood was premier, in one of the most unseeing and saddest contracts ever entered into by a sovereign state, he gave away the hydro's resources of the Upper Churchill Falls to the Province of Quebec for 65 years. The conditions of that contract mean that the company that operates the Upper Churchill would be bankrupt in another five or six years in any event because it will not be able to keep up with the inflation which set in in the last ten or 15 years. But I will set that aside for tonight, Mr. Speaker, as I want to concentrate on the offshore minerals problem.
The government prepared its case. Let me explain to the Ftouse that the case will not depend on the question of legal ownership. If any court in the land makes a pronouncement on who technically, legally owns those resources, that is not going to settle the issue. If the Supreme Court of Canada, because it wants to follow the decision it made with respect to British Columbia around 1967 and decides that it does not want to trouble the waters and cannot afford not to be uniform one coast with another-if it decides on technical and legal grounds that the Government of Canada owns the resources, it should not be thought that this will settle the issue. The only thing that will settle the issue is a political arrangement that is satisfactory to the people who brought those resources into confederation. Nothing else, Mr. Speaker.
Hear, hear!

The federal bully boys, the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) do not need to worry. The Supreme Court of Canada is not going to save their bacon. The only thing that can do that is an agreement that is satisfactory and in the spirit of confederation-an agreement that meets the test of a federal state. The test is that in a federal state of Canada, in our confederation, resources are owned and controlled by the provinces.
Hear, hear!
The federal government has huge powers. We know that and we saw them exercised-
Oh, oh!

Gentlemen, just listen. Relax and learn. The federal government has gigantic powers. It could fight Alberta to a standstill. It has powers of direct and indirect taxation; it
has the powers of interprovincial trade; it has the powers of international trade-it has all kinds of muscle. We know that it would be a standoff and that the federal government could win, no matter who owns the resources. Nevertheless, it is very important for a province that it own the resources because then it can control the rate of development.
I will tell you something, Mr. Speaker. In Newfoundland we are never going to be a milch cow, milked dry because the federal government wants all our oil and gas in the next 20 years. Because it failed with the tar sands, it failed with Alsands, it failed with Cold Lake, it failed in the Beaufort Sea, it is not coming down to Newfoundland to haul out our oil and gas and minerals to make up for failures elsewhere!
Hear, hear!

Those resources have to be developed first for the good of the people who live in the surrounding area and who for 400 years have had to leave their homeland to get work. First, it has to mean something for them. First, it has to mean that the oil and gas industry is established in Newfoundland. First, it has to mean that our people are trained for the jobs, and the development must not be too fevered. It must not wreck urban development in Newfoundland. It must not wreck the services that had to be provided in Newfoundland for the development of the oil and gas. That is the first requirement. We are not going to allow it to be hauled out in the next ten or 15 years because the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has been bankrupt in his policy and now desperately wants to find oil and gas in Newfoundland and Labrador.
That brings us up to the time that the Progressive Conservative government came into power in June 1979. Until then the Liberal Government of Canada had refused to consider any kind of decent, meaningful agreement with the province. It said it owned the resources, was going to control them but this party and its leader who is sitting here tonight, the right hon. member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), adopted a policy-
Oh, oh!
I do not know what is so funny about that, gentlemen. They are not laughing over on these front benches when the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition asks them a question or two. They cringe.
Hear, hear!

We saw today, Mr. Speaker, the spectacle of the Minister of Finance, feckless, fearsome, frivolous, not knowing where to turn, frigid, frozen and frumpy, coming back from Versailles. It is a wonder he did not meet in the railway car over there in Versailles so he could surrender to Ronnie Reagan in decent obscurity. He could not answer a question; he was completely inconsistent. On one hand he is going to enlarge the deficit, he is going to be expansionary. On the other hand he reads the communique as though he were
June 8, 1982

the author. He had nothing more to do with it than the president of Lithuania, Latvia or Switzerland. They are going to regulate the deficits tightly and keep them down. Did you ever see a man so inconsistent, so desperate, so pleading, looking so bewildered? All the vim and vigour has gone out of the cunning little trimmer. Now that he is faced with the responsibility, he does not know where to turn. He is going from one end of the griddle to the other and he has nowhere to turn.
To come back to where I was on the offshore, our party, led by the right hon. member for Yellowhead, adopted this policy; our party does not care who owns, in a technical sense, the offshore resources. We care not a whit. If the court says the Government of Canada owns them, we will say fine, that is great and we will get on with solving the problem, because, as the then Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) wrote the Premiers of Canada in September, 1979, we take the position that it is in the spirit of confederation and of a federal state that the provinces should have the ownership and management of those resources in any event, just as Saskatchewan has the resources under its soil, just as Alberta, and Ontario do, so should Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and British Columbia have the resources under their soil and under the saltwater off their shores. That is our position, and when we return to power we do not care what that group of bully-boys opposite do with a Supreme Court of Canada decision, if there is one in their favour. We are going to say to Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, P.E.I., New Burnswick, British Columbia and Manitoba, and the others who have an offshore: gentlemen, we are proposing legislation and constitutional changes which will put you in the same position in which Canada put Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba during the 1920s. Canada owned the oil and gas and other resources under the soil of those provinces for technical and legal reasons, because it was part of Prince Rupert's Land or the Hudson's Bay Company or whatever. The federal government of the day owned those resources, but it saw that in a federation all provinces had to be treated the same and therefore it saw that the title was transferred to those three provinces. We are going to do the exact same thing with Newfoundland, Labrador, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. Even though we have to pull New Brunswick kicking and screaming to the table to accept it, we are still going to do it. British Columbia, Manitoba and Quebec, they will all be recognized as owners of the resources that lie off their shore because we think that is the federal system in Canada and we are not there to take advantage. We do not say, Mr. Speaker, that we believe in overcoming regional disparity and then, when a province has a chance to stand on its own two feet, make sure that its feet are taken out from underneath it and it does not even have the resources to do it.
Hear, hear!

The hallmark of this government is hypocrisy from end to end. From their foreign policy to their domestic policy, say one thing and do the opposite. Say to Newfoundland: yes, you are the second poorest province in Canada. I
Petroleum Administration Act
think the only one a little bit poorer than us is Prince Edward Island. They are not much under us, and we are fighting to be at the bottom. I remember, when Stuart Smith went around Ontario saying that Ontario was number ten, the deep spirit of resentment we felt in Newfoundland. Ontario was even going to claim to be number ten now. Well, the people of Ontario showed what they thought about old number ten, and he is now up in the Science Council of Canada, number $100,000 a year.
You want $100,000 a year?
I don't want any $100,000 a year from any Science Council of Canada, brother. All I want is a decent cabinet minister's salary and the chance to get this country back on the track again.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, we believe that no matter what happens in the next couple of years, we make the solemn commitment to Newfoundland and the other offshore provinces that no matter what the blackguards in this government do, no matter what the power grabbers do, no matter what the people who have declared war on the poorest of the Canadian provinces do, no matter what the Prime Minister, who says cooperative federalism is at an end, does, the man who wants to wage war in Canada but outside of Canada loves everyone, he is the soul of love for the governments of Russia and Poland, a man whose heart opens for all the east bloc countries, it does not matter what he does. It is only his fellow Canadians he gives the mailed fist to, as we discovered in Canada. We say to them: do your worst because we are going to reverse it. If you have a chance to do it, we are going to see that this confederation stands and that all of its parts have a fair deal.
Hear, hear!

That is because we have a leader who understands how this country operates. Oh, he is not a great theoretician like the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who wrote all those fine essays years ago, all those very fine academic exercises which showed us how he was going to lead us to the East European socialist economy which he is now carrying on. No, our leader understands that this is a federation and a community of communities. Of course, all the intellectuals in the media-and God knows we have a lot of them, particularly the national columnists-do not think much of that community of communities idea. They have some other great theory that what is good for central Canada is good for Canada. That is their theory. What is good for General Bullmoose is good for the country. What is good for Windsor is good for the country. Why, the minister in charge of overcoming regional disparity is from Windsor. As I said here in the House the other day, it is the equivalent of the Red Cross appointing Dracula as the blood transfusion supervisor. All he is interested in doing is stopping the Japanese cars coming into Vancouver by putting the customs men on them. That is the answer of our minister

June 8, 1982
Petroleum Administration Act
responsible for international trade. Here is a country more dependent on international trade than any other, Mr. Speaker. Thirty-three per cent of our GNP comes from international trade. Seventy per cent of our exports go to the U.S. and roughly 70 per cent of our imports come from there. They are big muscle men; they do not care about that. Why, they are going to tell Uncle Sam what to do with his deficit. They do not know what to do with their own but they are going to tell Brother Reagan what he should do with his, which is much lower than ours proportionately. Why, they are going to tell the Japanese what to do with their cars when we already have a trade surplus with Japan of over $1 billion a year. These big bold buckoes are going to tell the Japanese to take their cars and stick them up their customs sheds.
What is to happen to us if the Japanese then say they are not going to take our minerals and our lumber? FISHERIES-CLOSURE OF FISH PLANT AT GEORGETOWN, P E L (B) ROLE OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, H. B. Nickerson and Sons Limited have not reopened their Georgetown Seafoods Plant on Prince Edward Island for the current season, effectively eliminating over 500 jobs in the province at
June 8, 1982

one fell swoop. On Wednesday, June 2, in the House of Commons, I directed a question to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) about a proposal put by the Prince Edward Island government to the federal government to reopen the plant. The P.E.I. proposal would require the federal government, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans in particular, to allow a fish quota for the plant large enough to make it profitable to operate.
In the past, Georgetown Seafoods has been plagued by insufficient quantities of high quality fish for processing, as well as by high operating costs at a time of poor markets. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, in response to my question to him in the House of Commons, rejected the P.E.I. government's proposal. He did so on the grounds that an assured fish quota for the Georgetown Seafoods Plant would "have implied a dislocation in fish supplies to another area in the maritime provinces". The minister's concern was that the Georgetown plant should not be reopened at the expense of transferring fish licences from Nickerson and Sons Limited to a new owner or a new operator-especially if such a transfer would undermine the fishery elsewhere in the region, for example, in Cape Breton.
In my supplementary question I suggested to the minister that, if he was not prepared to accept the P.E.I. proposal to open the Georgetown Seafoods Plant, it was incumbent upon him to suggest an acceptable alternative plan because he had a vital role to play in reopening the facility and in assuring its long-term success. Again, the minister was concerned about, "taking licences away very arbitrarily from an area to put them into another area of the maritime provinces".
But the minister's concern is grossly misplaced. The fact is that any assured fish quota for the Georgetown Seafoods Plant-even if it involved a transfer of licences from Nickersons to another operator, and that may not be the case-would not seriously jeopardize fish supplies anywhere else. The Atlantic fishery is on its knees. Fish processing plants are closing all over the place. There is, consequently, an oversupply of fish for processing purposes. Why, then, would the minister be alarmed about the prospect of a few fish licences exchanging hands, particularly when Nickersons would be the ones giving them up? That company is fast getting out of the fish processing business. It is a matter of public record. Everyone knows that the company has taken steps to dispose not only of the Georgetown Seafoods Plant itself, but also of a number of licences that go with the plant. Even if that were not the case, and it is, what is sacrosanct about the existing disbursement of fish landing rights when fewer and fewer people are left in the industry to exercise those rights?
The P.E.I. government has devised an eminently reasonable strategy to rekindle the flame of prosperity at Georgetown. But the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has thrown water on it even before the match is lit, all in the name of some high principle which has no practical foundation whatsoever. The basic problem is that the minister approaches the issue of Georgetown Seafoods on a totally negative footing. Instead of saying, "Here is a plant, it must be opened and how do we do
Adjournment Debate
it?", the minister says, in effect, "We cannot do this and we cannot do that. My hands are tied." The minister's hands are not tied. He has the wherewithal to enable the Georgetown plant to open its doors again. There is no evidence that the Government of Nova Scotia-the very province whose interests the minister claims he is protecting in all of this-opposes the P.E.I. government's proposal to reopen the Georgetown plant. Surely that province would object if the Nova Scotia fishery were threatened in some way by the P.E.I. government's proposal. One can only assume that either the minister is unaware of the facts or is using the question of licences as a cop-out not to do anything.
Much more than the continued survival of a fish plant is at stake. The jobs and livelihood of some 500 people are hanging in the balance. Last year, income tax T-4 slips were issued by the plant to some 570 employees. The truth is that the entire Island economy will be affected by what happens or fails to happen in this matter.
Last week it was shown that P.E.I. experienced the largest percentage increase in unemployment from one month to another since the federal government began keeping unemployment records. That is the largest increase on record. Statistics Canada figures revealed that 15.5 per cent of the work force in the province of Prince Edward Island was unemployed in May compared to 12.5 per cent in April. The job picture would be improved substantially if Georgetown Seafoods were to get on its feet again.
I plead with the minister to play his part in saving the jobs of these fine people. Their future depends largely on his willingness to act. His failure to do so would constitute a most serious dereliction of duty.

before the provincial government to keep the plant open. I only wish that he displayed the same concerns with his provincial colleagues that he is portraying this evening. I further wish he had made those same kinds of representations to the provincial cabinet in late March and early April when that cabinet rejected the proposal which, if accepted, would have meant that the plant would be in operation today.
Now that the provincial government has approached the federal government seeking its assistance and intervention, and now that the federal government is actively exploring solutions for the future of this plant and for the industry throughout the region, I would like to caution the hon. member to ensure that his current involvement in the matter does not jeopardize those very sensitive negotiations that are going on.
We have been and are actively working to find a solution to reopen the plant, to put people back to work and to open up the market for these fishermen. Several alternatives are being carefully examined and so this evening I enjoin the hon. member to put aside whatever motivations may have prompted the question this evening and to work closely with us, with the federal government and with the provincial government, to see that the plant is reopened and its employees returned to work.
I therefore want to assure the hon. member that as a member of the federal government and as the representative of the people directly involved, everything possible is being done to reach an early solution. I welcome his interest and invite his continued involvement.

PUBLIC WORKS-REQUEST THAT CONSTRUCTION OF WASHINGTON EMBASSY BE POSTPONED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in early May it was revealed that a long-time friend of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was awarded the contract to design and oversee the construction of the Canadian embassy in Washington, D.C. Canadians are getting so used to political gifts to Liberal friends, that this political and government graft basically goes unnoticed. But it absolutely sickens me, Mr. Speaker, to see this happen at any time, but particularly my flesh seems to crawl when I see this happen at a time when the economy is in the state it is in.
I asked the Prime Minister on May 25 a very simple question:
Is the government or the Prime Minister considering postponing the design and construction of the embassy building in Washington because of the economic hard times facing Canada, with unemployment at an all time high, farmers going bankrupt, and small businessmen going bankrupt and, if not, why not?
The Prime Minister in his usual cavalier manner said "No, they were not changing their position." In fact, he chastised me because I had asked the same question, or basically the same question, on May 14.
It is a well known fact, Mr. Speaker, that in this country when people do not have the funds to spend they do not spend them. That is the kind of thing that we are hearing daily from
the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), saying, if you do not have it, then you do not spend it.
Businessmen right across the country who do not have the money to expand are not expanding and are not building the new buildings that are required to operate at so-called efficiency, because they do not have the funds to do it.
I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to consider for a moment the $38 million, approximately, that is to be spent, according to the Prime Minister, on the construction of an embassy in Washington, when the embassy staff at the present time are occupying perfectly adequate rented quarters, and could easily operate out of those quarters for the next five years, with absolutely no detriment to their jobs. Yet we in Canada, at this time, because the government, because the Prime Minister says so, Mr. Speaker, and will not look at the deficit and the deficit financing, are perfectly prepared to go to Washington, D.C. and spend somewhere around $38 million. When the architect Erickson gets on the job, that $38 million will increase to $100 million.
Leaving that aside, we go down to Washington and spend this money, money that the Canadian government does not have and will probably have to borrow on the foreign market in American funds at a high interest rate, putting more burden on the taxpayers of Canada-to create jobs in the United States, in Washington, D.C. Mr. Speaker, there is something basically, fundamentally, absolutely wrong, particularly when the Prime Minister, in his very cavalier way, says, and 1 would like to read you his answer from Hansard at page 17430:
-the work of the embassy staff is done in Washington, I believe, in a series of buildings-
"I believe"-in other words, he does not even know. He went on to say:
In view of the fact that the United States remains our most important economic and political power, it would seem to me that it is self-evident that a building housing all the embassy personnel which will make their work efficient and effective should proceed. I believe the amount involved is some $38 million, or a figure in that area. That is an imporant building. Madam Speaker, and as the hon. member knows, the Government of Canada is building more expensive buildings in various cities across Canada which are needed to ensure the federal government is able to discharge its services in various parts of the country.
1 can tell you, Mr. Speaker, they are sure not spending that kind of money to upgrade the facilities in my riding. They are not spending that kind of money to build an air terminal at Fort McMurray, that is now operating, for a city of 30,000 people, having to use construction trailers as a terminal building. They are not spending it in those areas, Mr. Speaker.
They are not spending that money on post offices, they are not spending it in a little place like Calling Lake, that requires something like $5,000 to upgrade its facility, so that the people do not have to wear overshoes and parkas in the wintertime when delivering the mail, when the postmistress goes to deliver the mail to the people coming in that area.
It is absolutely and totally ludicrous, Mr. Speaker, that this government would think at this time to go into massive capital expenditure in a foreign country, in any foreign country, when

the rental facilities are quite adequate to carry them over a period of five years until the taxpayers in this country can afford to spend the money. Mr. Speaker, 1 rest my case.

MULTICULTURAL1SM-SPEECH MADE BY CHAIRMAN OF RACE RELATIONS COMMITTEE. (B) MINISTER'S UNDERSTANDING OF MULT1CULTURALISM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 19, as reported at page 17589 of Hansard, 1 put a question in the House concerning remarks made by Israel Ludwig, the government-appointed chairman of the race relations committee of the Canadian Consultative Council on Multiculturalism. I have no doubt that Mr. Ludwig's remarks were sponsored by the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Fleming) and they echo what the minister himself has said. Pretending to criticize racism, these gentlemen attacked the basic freedoms and traditions of our society and demonstrated once again the government's intention to impose its will by restricting freedom.
Adjournment Debate
I do not think it was any accident that the minister in his evasive reply to my question made a cheap, derogatory remark which was extremely offensive to the ethnic communities in this country. It was particularly insulting to those people in the area 1 am proud to represent. It showed once again the lip service which this government pays to multiculturalism and its contempt for the variety of cultures other than English and French which make up this country.
Racism is brutal, inhuman and does not belong in a democracy. When we look at the record of this government, no one who has been around here since the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came on the scene should be surprised by this war against freedom. This government has pursued absolute power at the expense of democracy, Parliament, the press, free employment, business, labour, broadcasting and freedom of information. Through the gruesome Kent commission on newspapers, it is expanding the control of the media which it now exercises through the CRTC.
Dictatorship, by any other name, stinks in the nostrils of freedom-loving people. It always starts with the control of information. We should not forget the examples of Hitler's Germany, Franco's Spain, the Communist bloc-particularly Poland-and, yes, Argentina. It is all too easy to say it cannot happen here but, if we think just for a moment, we will know it is happening.
The manipulation of the press by the Minister of State for Multiculturalism should be seen together with his attempts to increase the censorship powers of the CRTC. They should be put together with the latest dirty trick of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) in the long line of Liberal ministerial attempts to influence justice, which are blessed and rewarded by the Prime Minister. We can add the deliberate avoidance of Parliament and the growing dominance of senior bureaucrats who are political appointees of the Prime Minister. And let us not forget the Prime Minister's carefully staged press conferences and the torrent of controlled information from government information departments. Above all, remember that this government spends hundreds of millions of taxpayers' dollars to cheat democracy by deceitful advertising.
Canadians elect Parliament in a democratic election, but apart from election day there is little democracy left. We have a democracy one day in every four or five years. The people's voice is heard once in every four or five years, and if the Prime Minister has his way, even that will disappear. Right now he ignores Parliament and boasts about it. Right now we have government by decree. One after another the orders in council pour out, dodging debate in this House and escaping the notice of the people. Cabinet ministers do not bother to tell Parliament about their sneaky schemes. The Minister of State for Multiculturalism did not tell Parliament what he and his bureaucrats are going to do to our newspapers. He told an audience at the University of Western Ontario. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) did not tell MPs what the government is going to do with the taxpayers' money they

June 8, 1982
Adjournment Debate
invested in CDC. The subterranean Senator Austin spilled it to the press.
There is no freedom of expression here unless you are a Liberal lackey. The government rammed the metric system down the throats of Canadians; not through Parliament but through a metric commission, a bunch of bureaucrats ordering Canadians what to do under threat of penalties and spending millions of taxpayers' dollars to brainwash Canadians. Metric was not introduced as it was in the United States or Britain or other democracies where people have a say in the affairs of their country. This government does not believe that Canadians can think for themselves, or be allowed to read what they want, or listen to what they please, or do whatever they like. Canadians are not asked by this government, they are told. Neil Fraser, a civil servant, had the guts to speak out against dictatorship, and he was fired. Like him, throughout history men who have tried to light the torch of freedom have been deprived of their civil rights, deprived of their jobs, put in prison, have suffered torture and oppression.
It cannot happen in Canada, you say, but it is happening right now. Ask Neil Fraser. Ask the judge who received the Solicitor General's letter. Ask the newspapermen and broadcasters, and ask those people who cannot get jobs because they do not speak a preferred language.
The Kent commission was appointed by the Prime Minister. Its chairman was a Liberal hack and former Liberal bureaucrat devoted to government intervention. One of the two other commissioners was a career bureaucrat who believes utterly in the CRTC. What a cynical response to concern about the press. Nobody should have been surprised that the commission came up with what the government wanted-more intervention, more government control. We have heard the Minister of State for Multiculturalism rejoicing in the possibility of limitations on press freedom. The Prime Minister has always wanted to muzzle the press.
Newspapermen are rightly furious when newspapers disappear, but the Kent Commission and the government have done absolutely nothing to improve newspapers or increase the number of newspapers.
No newspaperman worth the name should allow regulation of any kind, and the newspaper owners should have refused point blank to talk to the government. Their duty is clear, and if they exercise that duty they deserve their privileged position.
The people of Canada should be on their guard against interference with their newspapers. Whatever the evils of private ownership and the operation of free enterprise, they are far less dangerous than government interference. A completely
free press is an essential ingredient of a free society and an essential check on government.
Today, with an arrogant government led by power-crazed men, we need a free press. We need freedom. I hope MPs on all sides of the House will place freedom before party, and join together to stop the abuse of Parliament and the government's sinister attack on democracy.

The Minister of State for Multiculturalism stated at the time of Mr. Ludwig's speech, and has since said in the House, that he will not fire an advisory council member for expressing opinions.
On specifics, the minister has made clear that he disagrees with several of Mr. Ludwig's ideas. Although some of Mr. Ludwig's proposals have been misconstrued, the minister indicated at the National Symposium on Race Relations in Vancouver, and in the House since, that the government would disagree with any proposal to eliminate Christmas and Easter as Statutory holidays.
The minister is concerned that members know that Mr. Ludwig's comments were made in the context of a number of prominent Canadians from different segments of Canadian society exchanging views on race relations and the law. Police, civil libertarians, visible minority leaders, human rights commissioners and the other thoughtful participants, all agreed that the symposium was a useful exchange of ideas on ways to foster racial tolerance in Canada. If the hon. member for Edmonton North felt insulted, 1 believe the offending remark may have been a reference to pirogis. Anyone who thinks the minister of multiculturalism's good natured remark about pirogis was racist, obviously does not know the minister very well. Since the minister enjoys and views pirogis as part of Canada's multicultural wealth, he spoke without any wish to demean. Those who shouted racism must have felt there is
